title: What you are actually running
summary: GNU coreutils 9.4 on Ubuntu, the info manual, and the shell builtins that pretend to be the same tools.
text:
GNU coreutils is one package that absorbed the old textutils, fileutils, and shellutils collections. On this machine it is the set of programs that copy, list, sort, checksum, and format ordinary files. It is not the kernel, not the compiler, and not the shell. A C++, Rust, or Android build uses it constantly anyway: `install` places a binary, `nproc` suggests a job count, `sha256sum` checks an NDK archive, and `timeout` stops a hung test. Those are coreutils jobs. `grep`, `find`, `make`, and `adb` are not.

The introduction in the installed info file says the utilities are mostly compatible with POSIX, and that the info manual is the documentation the project maintains. It also says the man pages are no longer maintained. When a man page and the info node disagree, follow the info node for coreutils 9.4, then confirm the flag still exists in `--help` on the binary you will run. The HTML manual on gnu.org tracks newer releases. A flag you saw on the web and cannot find in `--help` is not a flag you have.

The shell sits in front of every command line. Bash provides its own `echo`, `printf`, `test`, `[`, `true`, `false`, and `pwd`. Those builtins do not have to match `/usr/bin` of the same name. The manual says this explicitly for `echo`: an unadorned `echo` may not be the program the chapter describes, and `env echo` is one way to skip the shell's version. This course uses absolute paths when the difference matters, and it shows `type` so you can see the shadowing on your own prompt.

Exit status is how these short programs talk back. The manual's rule for almost every command is that zero means success and non-zero means failure. It then lists exceptions whose statuses mean something narrower: `chroot`, `env`, `expr`, `ls`, `nice`, `nohup`, `numfmt`, `printenv`, `runcon`, `sort`, `stdbuf`, `test`, `timeout`, and `tty`. `sort -c` uses 1 to mean "not in order" and 2 to mean "I could not run the check". `timeout` uses 124 when it kills the child. `test` uses 1 as the answer "false". Reading a bare non-zero as "the tool is broken" will make you mis-handle all three.

Ubuntu does not install every name the GNU manual has a chapter for. On this image, `hostname` belongs to the hostname package, `kill` and `uptime` belong to procps, and `find` belongs to findutils. Teaching those binaries as if they were this coreutils 9.4 build would be a lie about the system you develop on. The reference marks them as companions. The lessons that need them say so in the example badge.

Performance shows up later as a property of a bottleneck: locale collation, a sort that spills, a pipe that block-buffers, a copy that cannot reflink. Nothing in this orientation lesson is a speed ranking. The useful habit is to ask which resource is scarce before you add a flag.

title: Quoting, globs, pipes, and status
summary: The shell rewrites the command line before coreutils sees it. Quoting, globs, pipes, and exit status are the four rewrites that matter.
text:
Coreutils programs receive an argument vector and, if you connect them, a stream of bytes. They do not see the quotes you typed. Bash parses those quotes, expands globs against the directory, splits unquoted variables on `IFS`, and only then calls `exec`. If a lesson command "does the wrong thing", the first question is whether the shell already changed the request.

Single quotes are literal. Double quotes allow `$` and backslash escapes. Unquoted text splits on spaces and expands `*`, `?`, and `[]`. A file named `a b.txt` is one argument only when it is quoted or when a glob produces it as one match. The glob `box/*.txt` is safe for spaces in the matched names because each match becomes one argument. It is unsafe for a name that starts with `-`, and it never matches a leading dot.

A pipe connects stdout of one process to stdin of the next. The default status of a pipeline is the status of the last process. `set -o pipefail` changes that: the status is the rightmost non-zero status. GNU `false` in the middle of a pipeline is invisible unless pipefail is on. SIGPIPE is the other half of this. A writer whose reader exits early receives SIGPIPE and, under pipefail, the pipeline often ends at 141, which is 128 plus signal 13. `yes | head` is the small version of that story. The later `yes` lesson measures it directly; here you only need the rule.

`--` ends options. `cat -- -n` reads a file whose name is `-n`. Without `--`, many GNU tools treat `-n` as a flag. The common-options node describes this convention. It is not universal in the outside world (`echo` is the famous exception, covered with `printf`), but it is the habit to use in this package.

The shell also has a size limit on the argument vector. `getconf ARG_MAX` is not coreutils. It is still the number that explains why `printf '%s\n' *` dies in a directory of build products while `find` streaming names does not. Coreutils can read NUL-separated names with `--files0-from` on `sort`, `wc`, and several checksum tools. That is the escape hatch when the glob no longer fits.

## Recipes

Pass file names from a Rust or C++ driver as separate `exec` arguments, not as one string you hope the shell will split. If you must go through `sh -c`, quote with `printf '%q'` from the coreutils `printf`, which the printf lesson demonstrates.

For a directory you do not control, prefer a NUL-safe producer. `ls --zero` is GNU coreutils. `find -print0` is findutils, and the safe-pipelines lesson shows both, labeled. Do not `ls | while read` a build tree. `read` splits on whitespace and the newline in a hostile name ends the record early.

## Tips and pitfalls

The runner for this course sets `pipefail` around every captured script. A script you paste into an interactive bash does not, until you set the option. When a captured pipeline exits 141 and your terminal exits 0, that is the option, not a different coreutils.

Unquoted `$var` is not a coreutils bug. If `var='a b'`, then `cat $var` asks cat for two files. Quote `"$var"`.

A failed glob in bash, with default settings, stays as the literal pattern if nothing matches. `nullglob` turns it into zero arguments, and `ls` with zero path arguments lists the current directory. That surprise is worse than an error. Leave `nullglob` off unless you have handled the empty case.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

Quoting costs nothing you can measure against file I/O. The performance failure mode is accidental work: a glob of a million object files builds a huge `argv`, the kernel rejects it with `E2BIG`, and the command never starts. Streaming names avoids that allocation. `getconf ARG_MAX` reports the limit on this machine; it is a kernel parameter, not a coreutils constant, and it is not a reason to claim one `ls` flag is faster than another.

title: Redirections, streams, and stdbuf
summary: stdout and stderr are separate, FILE buffering is not the kernel pipe buffer, and stdbuf cannot change programs that never use FILE streams.
text:
A coreutils process has the three standard descriptors the C library expects. The shell wires them up before `exec`. `>` redirects file descriptor 1. `2>` redirects file descriptor 2. `>/tmp/out 2>&1` makes both descriptors share the destination, and the order of those redirections matters because `2>&1` copies the current meaning of descriptor 1. None of that logic lives in `cat`. `cat` writes bytes to whatever descriptor 1 already is.

Buffering is a second mechanism, inside the process, on top of the kernel pipe. The C standard library accumulates `printf` output in a user-space buffer. When stdout is a terminal it is typically line buffered. When stdout is a pipe it is typically fully buffered, often 4 KiB or 8 KiB, so a reader sees nothing until the buffer fills or the process exits. That delay is not the kernel holding the bytes. The bytes have not been written yet. Tools that call `write` directly never enter this path.

`stdbuf` exists to change the FILE buffering mode before the command's `main`. On this Ubuntu build the `stdbuf` binary contains the strings `LD_PRELOAD` and `libstdbuf.so`, and the library is installed at `/usr/libexec/coreutils/libstdbuf.so`. The preload constructor runs first and calls `setvbuf`. The manual then lists two reasons the setting may not stick. `dd` and `cat` do not use FILE streams for their I/O. `tee` sets up its own buffering and overwrites the stdbuf choice. Line buffering on stdin is rejected because it is meaningless; this 9.4 build exits 125 and says so.

A latency difference is real for programs that do use `printf` and then wait. The benchmark page times a four-line C harness, not `cat`. If that sample's medians separate, the note says they separated on that harness. It does not say `stdbuf -oL` makes coreutils filters faster. Throughput and time-to-first-byte are different questions. Full buffering can be the faster way to push a large file through a pipe, and the wrong way to watch a progress line.

## Recipes

When a long pipeline looks stuck, check whether the producer is fully buffering. A progress line from a C or C++ tool that uses `printf` and no `fflush` will sit in the FILE buffer until it fills. `stdbuf -oL` is the non-invasive experiment, and only if the program uses FILE streams and does not reset them. If the program is Rust and it wraps stdout in a `BufWriter`, stdbuf does nothing: Rust is not the C library.

For logs you want to keep, redirect in the shell rather than asking every tool for an output flag. `tool >run.log 2>run.err` keeps diagnostics out of the byte stream you will checksum.

## Tips and pitfalls

`stdbuf -oL` on `cat` is a no-op in the sense the manual describes. The pipeline still copies bytes. You cannot conclude from a successful exit that buffering changed.

Status 125 means stdbuf itself failed. Status 126 means the command was found but could not be executed. Status 127 means it was not found. Those numbers are in the stdbuf node. Do not treat them as the command's own status.

`LD_PRELOAD` is ignored for setuid binaries. stdbuf will not change a privileged program, which is what you want.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

The kernel pipe has a capacity. The FILE buffer is in the writer. Filling an 8 KiB stdio buffer and then one `write` system call is fewer transitions than one `write` per line. That is why fully buffered output can use less CPU for a bulk copy, and why it feels late when you are watching a build log. `stdbuf -o0` forces a write per FILE operation and can raise system time on a chatty producer. title: Locale, collation, and LC_ALL=C
summary: LC_COLLATE decides what "sorted" means. LC_ALL=C is byte order, not a universal speedup, and it changes joins and checksums of nothing but the order of text.
text:
A locale is a bundle of rules for characters, collation, numbers, dates, and messages. Coreutils does not invent a private alphabet. The sort node says that unless you ask otherwise, comparisons use `LC_COLLATE`, and a line's trailing newline is not part of the comparison. Under `en_US.UTF-8` the letters `a` and `A` are primary-equal and the case difference is a later pass, so they group together. Under `LC_ALL=C` the order is the unsigned byte order: `A` (0x41) before `a` (0x61), and `B` before `a` as well.

`LC_ALL` overrides the individual `LC_*` variables. Setting only `LC_COLLATE=C` while leaving `LC_CTYPE` as UTF-8 is a sharper knife, and it is easy to get half-wrong. For a byte-oriented contract, set `LC_ALL=C` on that one command. Exporting it for an entire desktop session also switches messages and number formats, which is more than a sort script needs.

Tools that look at locale in ways people forget: `sort` and therefore anything that requires sorted input (`uniq` after a locale sort, `join`, `comm`); `tr` character classes such as `[:upper:]`, because `LC_CTYPE` defines which bytes are letters; `sort -n` and `seq`, because `LC_NUMERIC` can make the decimal point a comma; `date`, because `LC_TIME` names months; `wc -m`, because a character is not a byte once the encoding is UTF-8. Checksums do not consult collation. `sha256sum` of a file is the same in C and in en_US. If a checksum changed when you exported `LC_ALL`, you changed the bytes, not the hash.

`LC_ALL=C` is often faster for `sort` of large text because the collation is a simple comparison instead of a multi-level Unicode weight. The manual does not promise a ratio. The benchmark page runs a fixed 100000-line file under both locales and reports medians. If they separate, the note says they separated on that file in a warm cache. If they do not, the note says the run cannot rank them. Either result is allowed. Do not paste a blog's "C is always 10x" into a build script.

Byte order is also the wrong order for humans reading a dictionary, and the wrong order for version numbers (`sort -V` is its own lesson). Pick the order that matches the consumer. A `join` requires both files to be sorted by the same rule. Sorting one file in C and the other in en_US produces a disorder diagnostic, not a merged table.

### Character count is not the byte count

 


### A checksum ignores collation

 


## Recipes

Put `LC_ALL=C sort -u` in front of a manifest of file names when the manifest is a byte contract, for example a list of object files a linker will consume. Put the locale sort only when a person will read the list as a dictionary.

If a `join` fails with "not sorted", do not reach for `--nocheck-order` first. Re-sort both inputs with the same `LC_ALL`. The join lesson shows what the nocheck flag hides.

For numbers that must use a dot, run `LC_ALL=C sort -n` or `LC_ALL=C numfmt`. A teammate whose `LC_NUMERIC` uses a comma will otherwise see a different parse. This sandbox's locale uses a dot; the flag is still worth writing down so the script does not depend on that accident.

## Tips and pitfalls

`sort --debug` prints which locale rules it used, on stderr. That line is part of diagnosing a "wrong" order. It is not corruption.

`uniq` compares adjacent lines in the locale's equality, unless you set C. Case-folding with `uniq -i` is a further fold. Sort and uniq have to agree or the adjacency is meaningless.

Setting `LC_ALL=C` does not make UTF-8 data ASCII. It makes comparisons and some classifications byte-wise. `wc -m` under `LC_ALL=C` counts bytes rather than decoded characters. That is useful when you mean bytes, and surprising when you meant letters.

title: Spaces, newlines, NULs, and binary bytes
summary: File names are byte strings. Newlines and leading dashes break line-oriented tools. NUL is the delimiter that cannot appear in a name.
text:
A Linux file name is a sequence of bytes, not a Unicode string and not a line. The only bytes that cannot appear are NUL and `/`. Space, newline, quote, leading dash, and invalid UTF-8 are all legal names. Tools that split input on whitespace or newline are assuming a subset of that space. The assumption holds for a tree you created with boring names and fails for a tree you downloaded, unpacked, or let a user name.

GNU `ls` can show the danger instead of hiding it. `--quoting-style=shell-escape` prints a name you could paste back into bash, including `$'...` for a newline. `--zero` ends each name with a NUL and does not escape the bytes inside the name, because NUL cannot occur there. Those two options answer different questions. The first is for a human. The second is for the next program.

`wc --files0-from=-` reads a NUL-delimited list of paths. `sort --files0-from` and the checksum tools have the same idea. The producer and the consumer must agree. `ls --zero | wc -l` is wrong: `wc -l` counts newlines, and the NUL list may contain none. The safe-pipelines lesson connects the pieces. Here the point is the delimiter.

Binary files are the same issue one level down. `cat -A` is a text visualization: tab becomes `^I`, a newline becomes `$`, a NUL becomes `^@`. It is not a reversible dump. `od -An -tx1` is the dump. `sort` will read binary input because the manual says GNU utilities do not restrict the bytes inside a line, but a "line" still ends at newline, and a missing final newline is silently supplied by `sort`. A file that is one huge line becomes one record. That is a memory question, not a character-set question.

Android build trees and Gradle caches do contain spaces (`Application Support` is a macOS problem; `My Documents` style names and NDK paths with spaces show up on Linux too). Rust `OUT_DIR` is usually safe. A test fixture that only uses `file1` never exercises the bug your user will hit.

## Recipes

When a shell loop must visit names, use `find -print0` (companion) and `read -d ''`, or stay inside coreutils with `ls --zero` only if you accept that `ls` is not a recursive inventory tool. `ls` without `-A` hides dotfiles. `ls` without a path argument lists `.`, which is a different set from the files you thought you passed.

For a checksum manifest of arbitrary names, GNU `sha256sum --zero` writes NUL-terminated records. Matching check mode can read them back. The checksum lesson shows the text format first, because that is what download pages publish. Switch to `--zero` when names are allowed to contain newlines.

## Tips and pitfalls

Creating the newline name with an unquoted command substitution is itself a quoting hazard. The example quotes the substitution. Copy the quotes.

`ls` output is not a stable API. Columns, color, and quoting depend on whether stdout is a terminal. In this capture, stdout is a pipe, so you get the non-terminal format. A screenshot of an interactive `ls` will not match.

Binary-safe does not mean "use cat". It means "do not treat the stream as newline-delimited text unless you have decided that is the format".

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

NUL-delimited streams are not slower in any way that matters next to `stat` calls. The costly bug is correctness that forces a retry: a script that splits names, misses a file, and reruns a link. `ls` itself is a poor recursive walker because it stats every name to decide how to print, which is a syscall per entry. If you only need names, a dedicated walker (`find`, which is not coreutils) can do less. If you need sizes, you were going to stat anyway, and `du` or `stat` is the honest tool. Do not "optimize" by parsing `ls -l`.

title: Listing names with ls
summary: ls prints names and, when asked, metadata. The format depends on the destination, the quoting style, and which names you asked to include.
text:
`ls` answers "what names are here, and optionally what metadata the kernel will tell me about them." It is a presentation program. The info node spends most of its length on which names are included, how they are sorted, and how they are printed. Those are three separate choices, and the defaults change when stdout is a terminal: columns and, depending on the build and aliases, color. In a pipe, this GNU ls writes one name per line if you pass `-1`, and a compact format otherwise. Scripts should pass the format they need and not inherit an alias. `command ls` or `/usr/bin/ls` skips an alias. It does not skip a shell function of the same name; `type ls` tells you.

`-a` includes names that start with `.`, including `.` and `..`. `-A` includes dot names and skips `.` and `..`. That is the useful inventory of a directory you intend to copy. `-F` appends a classifier: `/` for a directory, `@` for a symlink, nothing for a regular file. The classifier is a character on the end of the name. Do not feed `-F` output to another tool as a path.

`-l` is the long format: mode, link count, owner, group, size, time, name. `-h` prints powers-of-1024 sizes with a suffix. The sort lesson's `-h` can order that output; `numfmt` can turn a raw byte column into the same idea with an explicit unit. `-S` sorts by size. None of these are a substitute for `stat -c` when you need one field.

`dir` and `vdir` are the same package. `dir` is an ls with a different default presentation. `vdir` is closer to `ls -l`. Scripts that call `vdir` because it "looks like" a long listing will confuse a reader who has only learned `ls`. Call `ls -l`.

`dircolors` prints shell code that sets `LS_COLORS`. Evaluating it is what makes `--color=auto` look like your theme. The colors are not in the file. They are in the terminal. A log file that captured color codes is full of escapes; pass `--color=never` when the consumer is not a terminal.

## Recipes

For a build directory you want to eyeball, `ls -l -h -S --group-directories-first` puts directories first and large artifacts at the top of the file list. That is a human view. For a program, use `stat` or `find` (findutils) with an explicit format.

If you must log a listing in CI, pin `--time-style=long-iso`, `--quoting-style=shell-escape`, `-1`, and `--color=never`. The log is then diffable except for timestamps you expected to change.

## Tips and pitfalls

`ls` without arguments lists the current directory. A script that does `ls $maybe_empty` when the variable is empty becomes "list `.`", which looks like success and shows the wrong tree. Pass `--` and quote, and handle the empty case.

`-R` is recursive presentation, not an archive and not a walk you can resume. It is also easy to mix with `-l` into a blob no parser should read.

Aliases in `~/.bashrc` such as `alias ls='ls --color=auto'` do not apply to `sh -c` scripts or to exec from Rust. They apply to your interactive prompt. Do not debug a script by comparing it with what you see after an alias.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`ls -l` stats every name it prints. On a directory of hundreds of thousands of build outputs that is a lot of `stat` syscalls, and it is still the wrong interface if the next step parses the columns. The cost is metadata, not the printing. `ls` of a single name is fine. Recursive `ls -lR` of a multi-gigabyte tree is an inventory you did not need if `du -s` or a build tool already knows the answer. No flag of `ls` changes the disk bandwidth of reading file contents, because `ls` does not read contents except when it must identify some special cases. Do not use it as a copy or a checksum.

title: stat, touch, and timestamps
summary: stat prints kernel metadata with a format string. touch sets timestamps. GNU and BSD spell those jobs with different flags, and ext4's type code confuses stat -f.
text:
`stat` reads the inode (and, with `-f`, the filesystem) and prints what you ask. The default multi-line layout is for a person. `stat -c` is for a script. Format sequences include `%s` size in bytes, `%a` mode in octal, `%A` mode in symbolic form, `%U` and `%G` owner names, `%u` and `%g` ids, `%F` file type, `%y` human mtime, `%Y` mtime as seconds since the epoch, `%n` the name, `%h` the link count, `%b` the number of allocated blocks, and `%B` the block size those blocks are counted in. `%b` times `%B` is the allocated space, which is not `%s` for a sparse file. The du lesson uses that pair.

`touch` creates an empty file or updates timestamps. `touch -d '2020-01-02 03:04:05 UTC'` sets both times to that instant on GNU touch. `touch -r other file` copies timestamps from `other`. `touch -c` will not create a missing file. None of this writes your data. A reproducible build that needs `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` still has to pass that into the compiler; `touch` only fixes the inode clock after the fact.

Filesystem identity is where this host is a good teacher. `df -T` on the capture disk reports `ext4`. `stat -f -c '%T'` reports `ext2/ext3`. GNU stat is not confused about the mount in a vague way: the kernel's statfs type code for ext2, ext3, and ext4 is the same historic magic, and the format sequence prints that shared name. Use `df -T` or `findmnt` (findmnt is util-linux, not coreutils) when you need the type string a person means. Use `stat -f -c '%s'` when you need the filesystem block size.

Timestamps you copy from another machine are not a security log. They are metadata the owner can set, which is exactly why `touch -d` works without being root. Do not authenticate a file by its mtime. Checksum the bytes.

## Recipes

In a C++ or Rust release job, after you `install` a binary, record `stat -c '%s %a' ` on the installed path if the package format cares about mode and size. Record `sha256sum` if the package format cares about bytes. Do not record the default `stat` paragraph into a machine-readable bill of materials; the column widths are not a contract.

To see whether two builds produced the same bytes, ignore mtime. `cmp` is diffutils, not coreutils. `sha256sum` is the coreutils answer, and `install -C` is the coreutils way to avoid bumping mtime when the bytes already match.

## Tips and pitfalls

`stat file >` redirection is a different file from `stat`'s operand. People overwrite the file they meant to inspect by pointing a redirect at it. Put redirects on a log name.

`%Y` is seconds. `%y` contains a space and a timezone. If you sort on `%y` as text you are not sorting by time once the format varies. Print `%Y` and `sort -n`.

`touch` on a symlink updates the target unless you pass `-h`. The link-count and symlink lessons cover the distinction. If you only remember one rule: metadata operations follow symlinks unless a flag says `-h` or `--no-dereference`.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`stat` is one syscall per call for a file, plus formatting. It does not read the file. Calling it in a shell loop over tens of thousands of names is slower than a language that calls `stat` in-process, because you pay for a process per file. That overhead is real and it is still not a reason to parse `ls -l`. If you need many metadata records, use a program that can do the loop internally (`find -printf`, which is findutils, not coreutils) or call `stat` from Rust. `touch` is not a performance tool. Setting timestamps on an entire tree with a shell loop is dominated by process startup, the same way.

title: mkdir, rmdir, and empty trees
summary: mkdir -p builds parents under the umask. -m applies to the last component. rmdir only removes empty directories.
text:
`mkdir` creates directories. `mkdir -p a/b/c` creates each missing component and succeeds if the final one already exists as a directory. The mode argument `-m 700` is applied to the directory that the invocation treats as the one being created at the end, not to every parent it had to materialize. Parents are created with the mode `0777` modified by the umask. This capture environment's umask is `0022`, so a parent lands at `0755` while the leaf you named with `-m 700` lands at `0700`. That is the bug behind a "private" cache directory whose parent is world-executable and world-readable. If the parent must be private too, `mkdir` it separately with `-m 700`, then create the child.

`rmdir` removes a directory only when it is empty. A regular file fails with "Not a directory". A directory that still has an entry fails with "Directory not empty". Those are different mistakes. `rmdir -p a/b/c` removes `c`, then `b`, then `a` if each becomes empty. It stops when one is not empty. It will not delete a file that happens to sit in the way. That is why it is safer than `rm -r` for tearing down a scratch tree you believe is empty. If `rmdir` fails, something is still there and you should look before you reach for `-r`.

`mkfifo` creates a named pipe and is covered with tee. `mknod` can create a fifo too, and it can create device nodes if you pass a major and minor number. Device nodes in `/dev` are not a coreutils exercise and they need privileges. The reference entry says so. This lesson does not call `mknod`.

Directories themselves have a size, but that size is the directory's own metadata storage, not the sum of the files inside. `du` is the tool that walks. `stat -c %s` on a directory is almost never the number you wanted in a disk-usage report.

title: basename, dirname, readlink, realpath, pwd
summary: These tools rewrite path strings. They do not all require the file to exist, and the shell's pwd is not always /usr/bin/pwd.
text:
Path tools are string and symlink resolvers. `basename /src/libfoo.a .a` prints `libfoo`. `dirname /src/libfoo.a` prints `/src`. Multiple arguments are allowed on GNU basename and dirname. `-z` changes the output separator to NUL. It does not switch the tools into a mode where they read NUL-separated stdin. If you have a NUL list, you still need something that splits it and passes arguments, or you stay in a language that has the bytes. People pipe `find -print0` into `dirname` and get "missing operand", which is what this package does.

`realpath` prints an absolute path. By default every component except the last must exist. `-e` requires the last component too. `-m` allows missing components in the middle, which is how you ask "what would this path be" before you create it. `--relative-to=DIR` prints the result relative to DIR. That is the form you want in a build log that should not embed the absolute sandbox path, when both paths share a root.

`readlink` without flags prints the immediate target of a symlink and fails on an ordinary file. `readlink -f` canonicalizes, following every symlink, and all but the last component must exist. On a missing final component it still prints a path and exits 0. `readlink -e` is the strict form. `readlink -m` allows missing components. If you only want "is this a symlink, and what does it store", do not pass `-f`. `-f` answers a different question: the canonical file name.

`pwd` is a builtin in bash. `/usr/bin/pwd` is coreutils. `-L` is logical and follows the shell's idea of `$PWD`. `-P` is physical and resolves symlinks. In a directory you entered through a symlink, they differ. Build scripts that compare paths should pick one and document it. `realpath -P` is the physical resolution if you already have a path in a variable.

None of these tools create or delete the file, except that your script might do that around them. `mkdir -p "$(dirname -- "$path")"` is the usual pairing, and the `--` matters when the path starts with a dash.

In a script that receives a path from a user, run `realpath -e -- "$path"` when the file must already exist, and fail the build if it does not. Use `realpath -m` only when you are about to create the path and you need the absolute form for a log line.

`basename -- "$0"` is a common way to get a program name. The `--` is load-bearing if the name can start with a dash. Pair `mkdir -p -- "$(dirname -- "$dest")"` with `install -D` when you would otherwise recreate the parent logic by hand. `install -D` creates leading components itself; the permissions lesson prefers it for placing a binary.

Build systems should store relative paths in committed files. `--relative-to` the repository root keeps a CI workspace prefix out of the artifact.

## Tips and pitfalls

`dirname` of a name with no slash prints `.`. Feeding that to `mkdir -p` creates a directory in the current working directory, which may be correct and may be a surprise.

Command substitution deletes trailing newlines. A path that legitimately ends in a newline, which is rare and legal, will be damaged by `path=$(realpath -- "$path")`. NUL-delimited APIs avoid that. Coreutils `realpath -z` ends the output with NUL.

The builtin `pwd` can be a shell function's view of the world. If a script's shebang is bash, `pwd` is the builtin even when `/usr/bin` is first on `PATH`. Type the absolute path when you are teaching or testing the coreutils behavior.

These tools are string and symlink operations. `realpath` may call `lstat` on each component. That is noise next to compiling a crate, and it is the whole cost if you call `realpath` once per file from a shell loop over a million paths. Resolve a root once, then join relative names in-process if you are in Rust or C++. Do not cache a `pwd`

title: cp, sparse files, and reflinks
summary: cp can share data, preserve holes, or read every byte. On this ext4 disk a reflink clone is refused and a sparse file is not.
text:
`cp` reads a source and writes a destination, unless the filesystem can do better. "Better" has two independent meanings. A reflink or clone is a new directory entry that shares the source's data blocks until one side writes. A sparse copy is a destination whose holes are not written out as zero bytes. Neither is a guarantee. Both depend on the filesystem and on the flags.

On this machine `cp --reflink=always` fails with "Operation not supported". The capture disk is ext4, which does not do reflink clones. `--reflink=auto` is the default-ish polite request: try a clone, and if the kernel refuses, copy the bytes. `--reflink=never` forces the byte copy. A script that requires a clone, because it is about to mutate one side of a huge image, must pass `--reflink=always` and treat a non-zero status as "do not pretend these files are independent". A script that only wants a copy should pass `--reflink=never` when a silent clone would surprise a later checksum of allocated blocks, or leave the default if either result is acceptable. Say which one you mean.

Sparse files are a different axis. `truncate -s 1M` creates a hole. `stat` shows a large `%s` and a small `%b`. `cp --sparse=auto` uses a heuristic to keep holes. `--sparse=always` tries to make a sparse destination even when it has to detect zero runs. `--sparse=never` writes the zeros. `du -B1` without `--apparent-size` reports allocated space. `du -b` reports apparent size. If those numbers match, you do not have a hole.

`-a` is archive mode: recursive, preserve links as links, and preserve attributes. Copying a symlink with `-a` copies the symlink. `cp -L` follows it and writes a regular file. That choice matters for a toolchain sysroot, where a symlink to a shared library must stay a symlink.

`-n` / `--no-clobber` on this 9.4 prints that the behavior is non-portable and may change. The replacement the help text names is `--update=none`. `mv -n` does not print the same warning and exits 1 when it refuses. Do not assume the two `-n` flags are one feature.

`--parents` recreates the source path under the destination directory, but the source path is interpreted relative to the current directory. The example `cd`s first. Running it from the wrong place looks like a missing `src`.

## Worked examples

### Reflink request versus fallback

 


### A symlink stays a symlink under -a

 


### Sparse size versus allocated blocks

 


### Do not clobber, without -n

 


## Recipes

For an Android `out/` tree or a Rust `target/` directory, `cp -a` is the blunt instrument that preserves symlinks and modes. It is not incremental. `rsync` is the incremental tool and it is not installed here and not coreutils. If you only needed a clone and the filesystem is btrfs or XFS with reflink, `--reflink=always` is the cheap copy. On this ext4 host it is not available, so the cheap copy does not exist and you pay the bytes.

`--parents` is how you lift `include/foo.h` into `dest/include/foo.h` without rewriting the path in the shell.

## Tips and pitfalls

`cp dir1 dir2` when `dir2` exists creates `dir2/dir1`. When `dir2` does not exist, it creates `dir2` as the copy. `-T` forces "destination is the directory itself, not a container". Use `-T` in scripts that must not nest by accident.

Preserving ownership requires privilege. `-a` asks to preserve it and, as an ordinary user, will keep the owner you already have and may warn about what it cannot copy. Read stderr. A zero status can still have skipped an xattr or a capability.

Confirm a copy with `sha256sum` of both names. Matching digests means the bytes match. They do not tell you whether the filesystem cloned the extents or wrote new ones; `stat` block counts are the clue for holes, and this ext4 host simply cannot reflink.

## Exercises

A reflink is a metadata operation. A byte copy moves every byte through the page cache and may write them back. On a filesystem that supports reflinks, the difference is enormous

title: mv on one filesystem and across two
summary: mv is a rename when the destination is the same filesystem. Across devices it copies and then unlinks. -n refuses to replace and exits 1.
text:
`rename(2)` changes a directory entry. It is atomic on one filesystem and it does not copy bytes. `mv` uses it when source and destination are on the same device. When they are not, the kernel returns EXDEV and `mv` copies, then unlinks the source. That second form is not atomic. A crash in the middle can leave both copies, or the new copy without the mode bits you expected. Scripts that move a finished artifact into place on the same filesystem get the atomic publish. Scripts that move from the build disk onto a tmpfs ramdisk, or onto another mount, do not.

You can see the device identity with `stat -c '%d'`. Two paths with the same device number can still be different mount points in exotic setups, but a different device number is enough to prove the move cannot be a pure rename. This sandbox lives on the ext4 root. `/dev/shm` is tmpfs. The example moves a small file between them and prints both device numbers, then deletes the tmpfs file. Do not leave scratch files in `/dev/shm`.

`-t DIR` means "every operand is a source, and DIR is the container". That is the form that works with `xargs` (findutils, not coreutils), because you can put `-t` before the names `xargs` appends. `-T` means "the destination is not a directory to move into, even if it is a directory". Without `-T`, `mv file existing-dir` puts `file` inside `existing-dir`. With `-T`, that shape is an error unless you are replacing a non-directory. Pick one explicitly in a script.

`-n` refuses to replace an existing destination. On this GNU mv it prints "not replacing" and exits 1. The source remains. `--update=none` is the related cp spelling; mv's `-n` did not print the cp portability warning in the probe for this course. Still prefer the long option you can explain. `--backup` makes a backup according to the version-control rules in the common-options chapter. It is easy to fill a directory with `~` files if you turn it on in a loop.

Trailing slashes matter. `mv file dir/` insists that `dir` is a directory. The trailing-slashes node in the manual is the reference. A script that adds the slash fails closed when `dir` was accidentally a file.

Publish a finished archive by writing it to a temporary name on the same filesystem and then `mv -T` it onto the public name. Readers see the old file or the new file, not a partial write. If the public name is on another mount, you cannot have that atomicity. Copy to a temporary name on the destination filesystem and `mv` there.

`mv -n` in a loop is a reasonable "do not smash an existing artifact" check because the status is non-zero. Test the status. A script with `set -e` will stop, which is what you want if replacement is a bug.

## Tips and pitfalls

`mv` of a directory onto another directory moves it inside, the same way as a file. `mv a b` when both are directories yields `b/a` if `b` exists. That surprise has eaten release directories. `-T` makes the intent visible.

Cross-device `mv` of a symlink copies the symlink or the content depending on flags, and it may not preserve every attribute an ordinary user cannot set. Read stderr.

The trap in the cross-device example removes the shm file even when a later command fails. Copy that pattern. The course runner also deletes its sandbox, but `/dev/shm` is outside the sandbox.

## Performance

People "speed up" a script by switching to `mv` and then point it at another mount, where it is suddenly a full copy. Check `stat -c '%d'` when a move of a large Android image is mysteriously slow. There is no flag that makes EXDEV cheap. Reflink copies, where the filesystem supports them, are a `cp` feature, not an `mv` featur

title: rm, prompts, and shred's limits
summary: rm unlinks directory entries. -I can exit 0 without deleting. shred overwrites only when the device actually stores the new bytes in place.
text:
`rm` removes a name. When the link count hits zero and no process has the file open, the filesystem may reuse the blocks. It does not promise to erase them. `rm` of a file you have open in another process removes the name and leaves the data alive until the last file descriptor closes. That is why deleting a log that a daemon still has open does not free the space. The space shows up in `du` of the directory as gone and in `df` of the filesystem as still used. The du and df lesson is the measurement. The mechanism is the inode reference count.

`--` ends options, so `rm -- -rf` removes a file named `-rf` and does not recurse. Build this habit before you interpolate a variable. `rm -r -- "$dir"` is the shape. `rm -r $dir` is the shape that word-splits and glob-expands.

GNU rm treats `/` specially. `--preserve-root` is the default. `--no-preserve-root` turns the guard off. This course does not run either form against the real root. The help text is enough to show that the guard exists, and a demonstration that "probably refuses" is not something to type against `/`. The manual's node on treating `/` specially is the citation. If you need to empty a scratch directory, point `rm -r` at a path you created with `mktemp -d` and checked with `realpath`.

`-i` prompts for each removal. `-I` is less chatty: it prompts when you ask it to remove more than three arguments, or when you descend recursively. In this sandbox, `rm -I` on four files, with empty stdin, printed a question, deleted nothing, and exited 0. A `set -e` script will not notice. If you automate `-I`, you have not built a safety check; you have built a prompt that an empty pipe answers by keeping the files and looking successful. Prefer a dry run that lists names, then an explicit `rm` without `-I`, over a prompt nobody is watching.

`shred` overwrites a file's bytes and, with `-u`, unlinks it. The manual's assumption is that the filesystem and the hardware replace those blocks in place. It then lists designs that break the assumption: journaled data modes, copy-on-write and log-structured filesystems, snapshots, RAID, compressed filesystems, and wear leveling on SSDs, which write the new data somewhere else and leave the old data until garbage collection. ext4 in the default `data=ordered` mode is one of the cases the manual says still overwrites file data as usual, and `data=journal` is not. If you do not know the mount options, the manual tells you to assume shred cannot reliably operate on regular files. The example uses `-n 1` on a scratch file so you can see the name disappear. It is not evidence that a secret is gone from the device.

The manual's own advice points at destroying media when the bytes must be unrecoverable, and at full-disk encryption so the deletion problem is "drop the key" rather than "overwrite the NAND". Encryption is not a coreutils feature. It is the reason not to oversell `shred`.

## Tips and pitfalls

`rm -I` exiting 0 with the files still present is the sharp edge. Test the listing, not only the status, if you ever script `-I`.

`grep` in the help example is the grep package, not coreutils. It is labeled. The same line is visible in `rm --help` without grep if you read it; the filter keeps the capture short.

`shred` of a symlink shreds the target if it follows the link. Know what the name points at before you pass `-u`.

title: Hard links, symlinks, ln, link, unlink
summary: A hard link is another name for the same inode. A symlink is a path stored as data. ln -r rewrites that path to be relative.
text:
A hard link is a directory entry that points at an inode. Two names, one inode, one set of bytes, one link count. `stat -c '%h'` prints that count. When you `rm` one name, the count drops and the bytes remain while any name or open file descriptor remains. Hard links cannot span filesystems, because the inode number is local to the device. `ln` across devices fails. Hard links to directories are rejected for an unprivileged user; the kernel returns EPERM. `link` is the bare syscall wrapper and produces that error on a directory. `ln` is the tool with the useful flags.

A symbolic link is a file whose content is a path. The path is not checked when the link is created. It is interpreted when someone opens the link. `readlink` prints the stored path and does not follow further. `readlink -f` resolves it. If you store an absolute target, moving the tree to another prefix breaks the link. GNU `ln -s -r` / `ln -sr` stores a relative target computed from the link's location. That is what you want inside a project tree you will relocate. `cp -a` copies the symlink as a symlink. `cp -L` follows it. Those were captured in the copy lesson; the distinction belongs next to this one.

`ln -sfn new target-name` replaces a symlink even when the name already exists. Without `-f`, ln refuses. Without `-n`, some cases treat an existing symlink-to-directory as a directory to link inside. `-n` / `--no-dereference` is the "do not treat the destination as a directory" flag. The combination `-sfn` is the usual retarget.

`unlink` removes one name via `unlink(2)`. It does not take `-r` and it does not remove a directory. `rm` is the tool with those behaviors and with prompts. Use `unlink` when you mean exactly one non-directory name and you want a failure if that is not what you have.

`du` counts a hard-linked file once unless you pass `-l`. Two names are not two copies of the bytes. The disk-usage lesson measures that. Installing a binary with hard links to save space is a real packaging trick and a real surprise when you edit one name and the other changes.

For a system prefix, an absolute link under `/usr` can be correct because the target is supposed to stay at that absolute path. Decide which world the link lives in before you let `ln -s` store whatever string you were holding.

When a Rust `target` directory hard-links identical artifacts, `du -s` without `-l` is the honest disk usage and `du -l` is the sum of the names. Publish the one your capacity planning means.

`ln -s target link` does not read `target`. A typo creates a dangling link and exits 0. `readlink -e` is the check that every component exists.

Replacing a symlink with `ln -sf` while a running program has already resolved the old target does not change what that process has open. Symlinks are resolved at open time.

title: chmod, chown, and install
summary: chmod changes mode bits. chown changes ownership and fails here without privilege. install copies a binary into place and can skip the write when the bytes already match.
text:
The mode is a set of bits stored on the inode: read, write, execute, for owner, group, and other, plus setuid, setgid, and sticky. `chmod 640 file` sets owner read-write, group read, other nothing. `chmod u=rw,go= file` is the same request in the symbolic grammar, which is what you want when you are editing rather than replacing the mode. `chmod --reference=other file` copies the mode. It does not copy the owner. The reference file is dereferenced if it is a symlink, so you copy the target's mode.

`chown user:group file` changes ownership. Only a privileged process can give a file to another user. In this sandbox `chown 0:0` fails with "Operation not permitted" and exits 1. That is the correct outcome, not a broken chown. `chgrp` can change the group to another group you belong to. `--from` on GNU chown avoids a race where you only want to change the owner if it is still the owner you think. `--reference` copies both user and group. None of these change the bytes.

`install` is `cp` plus the modes you want for a published binary, with a few extra contracts. `install -D -m 755 src dest/bin/tool` creates the parent directories of the destination and sets the mode. `install -C` compares the content and does not rewrite the destination if it already matches, which leaves the mtime alone. Build systems use that so a later step does not rebuild the world because a timestamp moved. `-s` strips symbols and needs a `strip` program; this lesson does not strip, because stripping is binutils, not coreutils, and it changes the bytes.

SELinux context is a third channel. `chcon` and `runcon` are coreutils, and they need a kernel with SELinux. `id -Z` on this host fails because the kernel is not SELinux-enabled. A mode of 644 is not a substitute for a context, and a context is not a substitute for a mode. On this machine you only have the mode.

Directories need the execute bit to be traversed. A directory mode of 600 lets the owner read the directory's names and not traverse it usefully in the way people expect from files. `chmod` on a tree with `-R` will happily clear execute on directories if you apply a file-shaped mode. Do not `chmod -R 644` a source tree.

### install -D and install -C

A Rust or C++ release script should `install -D -m 755` the binary into the prefix rather than `cp` plus a separate `chmod`. The mode is part of the publish. Use `install -C` when the same script may run twice and you do not want to bump mtimes that a package diff will treat as a change.

Do not chown build outputs to another user in CI. If the package format needs root ownership, that is a packaging step with privilege, outside this sandbox, and it should be explicit. A failed chown in the log is better than a script that ignores the status and ships a root-owned path it did not create.

## Tips and pitfalls

`chmod` follows symlinks to change the target's mode. `chmod -h` is not portable. GNU chmod's `--help` documents how symlinks are handled; do not assume a mode change on the link itself.

`install -d` creates directories. `install -D` on a file creates leading components of the file destination. Mixing them up produces a directory where you wanted a file, or the reverse.

The mtime comparison in the example prints two integers. If they match, `-C` did not rewrite the inode's mtime. If a filesystem's timestamp granularity ever made them match by accident, the content comparison is still what `-C` did; the printed integers are the observation on this run.

title: dd, truncate, and sync
summary: dd copies blocks and can leave holes. truncate sets a size. sync asks the kernel to flush caches and does not prove the drive finished.
text:
`dd` reads blocks and writes blocks. The historical interface is `if=`, `of=`, `bs=`, `count=`, and `conv=`. It is easy to destroy a device by pointing `of=` at the wrong node. Every example in this lesson uses a regular file in the scratch directory. There is no example with `/dev/sd` or `/dev/nvme`. If a real disk image job needs `dd`, the destination path should be a file you just created, and the script should print that path before it writes.

`status=none` keeps the statistics off stderr. `status=progress` prints them. GNU dd's `iflag=fullblock` accumulates a full input block when the reader returns short reads, which happens on pipes. Without it, `bs=1M count=1` on a pipe can stop after the first short read and produce a short file. Copying a regular file in this lesson does not hit that case. Know it before you `dd` from a pipe and think `count` means what it means for a disk.

`conv=sparse` tries to seek over NUL output blocks instead of writing them. A file of zeros produced that way has a large size and zero allocated blocks on a filesystem that supports holes. `truncate -s 1M file` creates the same shape without writing the zeros at all. `truncate -s 0 file` empties a file but leaves the directory entry, unlike `rm`. Shrinking discards the tail from the file's logical size. It does not shred it.

`sync` asks the kernel to write out cached data. With no arguments it applies broadly. `sync -f file` syncs the filesystem that contains `file`. `sync -d` limits itself to file data. None of these calls can promise that a drive's own cache has committed the bits to stable media. They are still the right call at the end of a snapshot script, followed by an honest sentence in the log: the kernel was asked to flush. Durability beyond that is a property of the hardware and the mount options, which this course does not tune and does not drop caches to measure.

`od` is how you look at a small `dd` result when you care about bytes. `stat -c '%s %b'` is how you look at sparseness. `du -b` versus `du -B1` is the same story from the disk-usage tools.

## Worked examples

### A counted copy

 


### conv=sparse on zeros

 


### truncate extends without writing

 


### sync the filesystem that holds the file

 


## Recipes

Build a sparse disk image for a test with `truncate -s 64M image` only when 64 MiB is a size you are willing to create, and prefer a few megabytes in a sandbox. Fill a region later with `dd conv=notrunc` if you must write at an offset. `seek=` skips output. `skip=` skips input. Write both names down in the script so a reader does not swap them.

At the end of a backup that must survive power loss at the kernel level, `sync -f` the destination directory. Then say in the operator log that device firmware caches are outside that call.

## Tips and pitfalls

`/dev/zero` is not a coreutils invention. It is an infinite source of NUL bytes. `count=` is what makes `dd` stop. Forgetting `count` while reading `/dev/zero` fills the disk. The examples always pass `count`.

`status=progress` writes to stderr and will dirty a captured byte stream if you merge the descriptors. Keep it on stderr.

`truncate` on a missing file creates it. `truncate` on a symlink follows the symlink. Check `readlink` first if the name might not be a regular file.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`dd` with a tiny `bs` on a large file makes more syscalls than `bs` of 64 KiB or 1 MiB. The copy benchmark uses 64 KiB on an 8 MiB warm file and compares it with `cp`. Read the medians before you conclude anything. A larger block size can be slower if it causes a short-read bug on a pipe without `fullblock`, because you retry logic you did not write. Sparse conversion saves write I/O only when the output blocks are actually zero. A sparse `truncate` saves the writes entirely because nothing is copied. `sync` forces writeback, which makes a following read of "cold" data less cold and makes a benchmark that forgot about it lie. This course does

title: cat and tac
summary: cat streams bytes forward. tac reverses records. Neither one parses the file, and tac's separator stays glued to the record.
text:
`cat` concatenates files to stdout. With no file, or with `-`, it reads stdin. It does not transform the bytes unless you ask. `-n` numbers lines. `-s` squeezes repeated blank lines into one. `-A` is the "show me the hidden bytes" mode: tabs as `^I`, ends of lines as `$`, and other nonprinting bytes in caret notation, including NUL as `^@`. The output of `-A` is not the original file. Do not checksum it and think you checksummed the input.

`tac` prints records in reverse. The default record is a line. It has to see the end of the input before it can print the last record first, so it is not a streaming tool in the way `cat` is. A multi-gigabyte file reversed with `tac` is a memory and temporary-space question. The manual does not give you a sort-style `-S` for it. If you need the last lines of a log, `tail` is the tool that seeks. `tac` is the tool that flips a small stream.

`-s` on `tac` sets the separator. The separator stays attached to the record. For the input `a,b,c` with separator `,`, the records are `a,`, `b,`, and `c`, and the reverse is `c` then `b,` then `a,`, which prints as `cb,a,` with no extra newline. That looks like corruption until you dump it. `od -An -tx1c` shows the commas are still there, attached to the following record in the reversed output. This is the behavior to teach, not a bug to "fix" by adding a newline and hoping.

A missing final newline is still data. `printf 'abc' | cat` writes three bytes and no newline. `wc -l` on that stream reports 0. `cat` did not eat a line. There was no newline to count. The wc lesson is the full version of that trap.

`cat` of a binary file to a terminal can scramble the terminal by writing control sequences. This course dumps binary with `od` or `cat -A` into a pipe, not onto a claimed tty. The capture environment's stdout is a pipe anyway.

## Worked examples

Number a snippet for a code review paste with `nl -ba` rather than `cat -n` when you also need the blank lines numbered in the style the nl lesson controls. `cat -n` is the quick version.

Reverse a short list of records you produced yourself, after you have decided the separator. Do not `tac` a log to "see the end". `tail` seeks. `tac` reads.

## Tips and pitfalls

`tac` on a file that does not end with the separator still prints the last partial record. The comma example has no trailing comma and no trailing newline. The dump is the authority.

`cat file1 file2 > file1` truncates `file1` before reading it. The shell opens the redirection first. Do not concatenate a file onto itself that way. Write to a new name and `mv` it on the same filesystem.

`stdbuf -oL cat` does not switch cat to line buffering. The buffering lesson says why. Repeating it here because people put stdbuf in front of cat in log pipelines and then argue about the flag.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`cat` is a sequential read and write. For a warm cache and a destination that is another file, `cp` is the tool that can ask the filesystem for a reflink or a sparse layout. `cat` will read and write the bytes. Using `cat` in a pipeline (`cat file | tool`) adds a process and a pipe for no transformation. The tool can open the file. That extra process is small and measurable only when the work itself is small; the benchmark page does not pretend otherwise. `tac` is the one that becomes expensive for large inputs because reversal needs the records available from the end. `tail` is the constant-time-ish choice for "show me the end" on a regular file, subject to the kernel's ability to seek.

title: head and tail
summary: head prints a prefix, including GNU negative counts. tail prints a suffix or follows a file. Follow mode needs a bound.
text:
`head` and `tail` cut a sequence of records. The default record is a line. `-n` selects lines and `-c` selects bytes. `head -n 2` keeps the first two lines. `head -n -1` keeps everything except the last line. That negative form is the GNU extension that deletes a trailer without a second pass you write yourself. `head -c -2` keeps all but the last two bytes. BSD head will not run these negative counts. If the script must be portable, do the trim another way and do not copy the GNU flag blindly.

`tail -n 1` is the last line. `tail -n +2` starts at line 2 and continues to the end, which is the usual "drop the header" operation. `tail -c 3` is the last three bytes. These are streaming from the point they start, except that finding the last N lines of a pipe requires buffering those lines because a pipe cannot be seeked. On a regular file, `tail` can seek near the end. That is why `tail` of a huge log is cheap and `tac` of the same log is not.

`-f` follows a file descriptor as it grows. `-F` follows by name: if the file is rotated and a new file appears under the same name, `-F` retries and switches. A capture that uses `-f` must stop. `timeout 1 tail -n +1 -f log` runs until the timer sends SIGTERM and then exits 124. The lines that were already in the file are printed first. Nothing in this course follows a log forever.

`-z` makes the record separator NUL. `head -z -n 1` keeps the first NUL-terminated record, including the NUL. That pairs with `sort -z` and `ls --zero` when names are the records. Mixing `-z` tools with newline tools splits the wrong places.

`head` closes the pipe early when it has enough input. The writer receives SIGPIPE. Under `pipefail`, a pipeline such as `yes | head` can exit 141. Without `pipefail`, you see head's status 0. The shell lesson introduced the rule. `yes` is where the 141 is captured on purpose.

Watch a build log interactively with `tail -F` so a rotation does not freeze the view. In CI, copy the finished log. Do not leave `tail -f` as the last step of a job without `timeout`.

## Tips and pitfalls

`head -n -0` is not "give me nothing" in the way a casual reading suggests. Read the help text before you invent a negative zero. Prefer an explicit positive count when you can.

`tail -f` on a file that is not growing still holds the process. The timeout is not optional in a sandbox.

Combining `tail -f` and a pipe to `grep` (grep is not coreutils) reintroduces block buffering in grep. The lines exist and you do not see them. That is the buffering lesson, not a tail bug.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`head` stops reading when it has enough. On a pipe, that saves the producer from generating the rest only if the producer honors SIGPIPE or a short write. A producer that ignores SIGPIPE and keeps computing wastes the work `head` tried to avoid. On a regular file, `tail -n 10` of a large log is a seek plus a small read. `cat | tail` throws the seek away and reads the whole file. Do not insert `cat`. Following a file is idle most of the time; the cost is the open file and the poll, which is fine for a person and wasteful as a permanent CI step. There is no timing number in this lesson because "how fast is head" on three lines is process startup, and the interesting case is the seek `tail` can do. Measure that on a file large enough to matter, on the filesystem you care about, with the benchmark method: repeated trials, warm or cold stated out loud.

title: Counting with wc
summary: wc counts newlines, words, characters, bytes, and the longest line. A missing final newline makes -l and your eyes disagree.
text:
`wc` counts. It does not define a "line" as "what a text editor shows". `-l` counts newline bytes. A file that contains `hello` with no newline has a last line in an editor and a line count of 0 from `wc -l`. A file that contains `hello\n` has a line count of 1. This is the most common off-by-one in shell scripts that check "did the program print a line". Print the bytes with `od` when the count surprises you.

`-c` counts bytes. `-m` counts characters under the current locale. For the two bytes of UTF-8 `é` (U+00E9), `-m` reports 1 and `-c` reports 2 when the locale is UTF-8. The help text says the order of selected counts is newline, word, character, byte, maximum line length. So `wc -m -c` prints the character count and then the byte count. Under `LC_ALL=C`, the character classification collapses toward bytes and `-m` will not save you as a Unicode counter. Set the locale on purpose.

`-w` counts words: non-empty sequences of characters delimited by whitespace, with the locale deciding what is whitespace and what is printable. `-L` is the maximum display width of a line, not the byte length. A tab's display width is greater than one. Do not use `-L` as a buffer-size calculator.

With more than one file, `wc` prints a total unless you change `--total`. `--total=never` suppresses it. `--total=only` prints only the total. `--files0-from=F` reads NUL-separated names from F, or from stdin if F is `-`. That is how you count lines in files whose names contain spaces without the shell splitting them. Empty files contribute zeros and still appear as names.

`wc` reads the whole input. There is no "stop at the first match" flag. If you needed the first match, you wanted `grep` (not coreutils) or `head`.

Count lines in a selection of files with weird names by writing a NUL list. `ls --zero` is not a full recursive inventory. `find -print0` is the companion that walks. Either way, the consumer is `--files0-from=-`.

## Tips and pitfalls

`wc` with no flags prints lines, words, and bytes. Scripts that parse the default three columns break when someone adds `-l` and the columns shift. Pass the flag.

The total line says `total`. If you add `--total=only`, you lose the per-file lines. Pick the one the next parser expects.

`wc -l` on a directory fails. It is not `du`.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`wc -c` can use the file size from metadata for a regular file in some cases, but you should not depend on a shortcut for a benchmark story. `wc -m` has to look at the encoding. `wc -l` has to look at every byte for newline. The wc benchmark runs `-c`, `-l`, and `-m` on a warm ASCII file of 200000 lines and reports whether the medians separate. On ASCII, `-m` and `-c` count the same quantity and `-m` may still do more work. If the run cannot separate them, that is the result. A file of multi-byte characters is a different experiment; do not reuse the ASCII medians for it.

title: split and csplit
summary: split cuts by size or into chunks. csplit cuts at a pattern. Round-robin mode distributes lines, so one line stays in one piece.
text:
`split` writes pieces of a file. `-l 2` means two lines per piece. `-b` means bytes per piece. `-d` uses numeric suffixes instead of letters. `-a` sets the suffix width. The default prefix is `x`. Pieces land in the current directory unless you pass a prefix path. A script should `cd` to a scratch directory or pass an absolute prefix so it does not scatter `x00` files through a source tree.

`-n N` splits into N byte chunks as evenly as it can. `-n l/N` splits into N chunks without breaking lines. `-n r/N` round-robins lines across N files. The input `abcdef` with no newline is one line. `split -n 3` produces three pieces of two bytes. `split -n r/3` puts that single line into the first piece and leaves the other two empty, because there is only one record to hand out. People use `r/N` expecting byte striping and then checksum the empty files. The mode is about lines. Name the mode in a comment next to the command.

`--filter` runs a command for each piece, with `$FILE` set to the piece name. It is a way to compress pieces without a second pass you schedule yourself. The filter is a shell command. Quote it. This lesson does not need a filter to show the cuts; the sort lesson uses an external program for a different reason.

`csplit` cuts where a pattern matches. `csplit -f p - '/^FOOT/'` on a file that contains a header and a `FOOT` line writes the pieces and prints their byte counts to stdout. Those counts are the tool's report, not a `wc` you have to add. `-z` suppresses empty pieces, which matters when the pattern matches the start of the file or matches twice with nothing between. Patterns are basic regular expressions. They are not PCRE, and they are not a JSON splitter. A JSON line file splits cleanly with `split -l` only because each record is already one line. The moment a record contains a raw newline, line split is wrong.

## Recipes

Shard a line-oriented log for parallel workers with `split -d -l 10000 -a 4 --additional-suffix=.log`. Workers must tolerate a boundary that is not a transaction boundary. If the transaction is multiple lines, `split` does not know. `csplit` can cut on a start marker you control.

`--filter='gzip > $FILE.gz'` compresses each piece. Test the filter on one small file before you point it at a disk you care about. A bad filter with `-` reading stdin can look like a hang.

## Tips and pitfalls

`split` of a file that is smaller than the chunk size still creates the pieces `-n` asked for, some of them empty in the round-robin case. Check sizes with `wc -c` before you launch a worker per file.

`csplit` without `-k` removes the output files if an error occurs mid-way. `-k` keeps them. The quiet flag `-q` suppresses the byte counts. Use it when the counts would pollute a log, and omit it when the counts are the verification.

Brace repetition `'{*}'` must be quoted so the shell does not expand it.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`split` reads the input once and writes the pieces. The cost is the bytes, plus a directory update per piece. A million tiny pieces is a metadata storm, the same shape as the rm lesson's many unlinks. Choose a piece size that matches the consumer, not a piece size of one line for a multi-gigabyte log, unless you have a reason to pay for millions of inodes. `--filter` starts a process per piece. That startup dominates when the pieces are tiny and disappears when each piece is large. `csplit` scans for the pattern. It is not a search index. If you only need "bytes 0 to N", `dd` or `head -c` avoids the regex. There is no parallel flag on split in the sense of `--parallel` on sort. Parallelism comes from processing the pieces afterward, and only if the pieces are independent.

title: fmt, fold, expand, nl, and pr
summary: These tools reflow, wrap, expand tabs, number lines, and paginate. They are byte and column tools, and fold can split a UTF-8 character.
text:
`fmt` joins and breaks lines so a paragraph fits a width. It is for prose. It will join short lines that look like one paragraph, which is the wrong thing to do to a table, a poem, or a source file. `-w` sets the width. `-p` keeps a leader such as `>` on mail quotes and reflows the text after it. The leader is not a comment syntax for every language. `fmt` does not know Markdown.

`fold` breaks lines that are already too long. `-w` is the width. `-s` prefers to break at spaces. `-b` counts bytes. On this UTF-8 locale, `fold -w 1` of the character `é` (bytes C3 A9) split the character across lines. The dump is in the example. Do not assume a "column" option keeps a multibyte character together. If you need a character-aware wrap, this is the wrong tool, and the observation belongs in the lesson so you do not discover it in a log file of names.

`expand` turns tabs into spaces. `-t 4` sets the stop. `-i` only converts leading tabs. `unexpand` does the reverse and will change a run of spaces into a tab only when it lands on a stop. Round-tripping is not identity unless the stops and the `-a` flag agree. A Makefile has meaningful tabs. Do not `expand` a Makefile and check it in.

`nl` numbers lines. The default body style skips blank lines. `-ba` is `-b a`, "number all lines", and it numbers the blanks too. `-w` sets the width of the number and `-s` the separator. It is a formatter for a listing you will read. It is not an index you should parse to edit the file.

`pr` paginates. The default page header includes the date and the filename, which makes output unstable. `-t` omits the header and trailer so the bytes can go to another filter. `-2` makes two columns. `-s,` sets the separator between columns. `pr` is not `paste` and not `join`. It fills columns down the page from one stream.

Show a tab that a test failed to preserve with `cat -A` after `expand`, so the failure is visible in a log that does not show a tab as whitespace.

Number a log excerpt you are pasting into a bug report with `nl -ba` so the other person can say "line 40".

## Tips and pitfalls

`pr` without `-t` puts the run date in the header. Two captures will differ. The example uses `-t`.

`fmt` treats a blank line as a paragraph break. A file of single-line records with no blanks may become one paragraph. Check.

`unexpand` can look like it did nothing when the spaces do not fill a tab stop. Dump with `cat -A` before you conclude the input had a tab.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

These tools are linear in the input and cheap next to a compiler. The performance issue is using them on data they will damage: `fmt` on a minified JSON line builds a "paragraph" and spends CPU to produce a file the parser rejects. `fold` on a multi-gigabyte minified line holds a long line. GNU tools do not impose a tiny line-length limit, so the memory cost is the line, not a fixed buffer you can ignore. `pr` with many columns buffers a page. For a huge file, cut the piece you need with `head` first. None of these is a parallel formatter. If you need a fast code formatter, it is not in coreutils.

title: cut, paste, and the CSV myth
summary: cut selects bytes, characters, or delimiter fields. It does not parse quotes. paste merges lines. Neither tool is a CSV library.
text:
`cut -f2 -d,` prints the second comma-separated field. Fields are numbered from 1. `-d` is a single character. `--output-delimiter` changes what is printed between fields you kept, which is how you turn a comma file into a tab file without `tr` eating commas you meant to keep inside a field. `--complement` prints the fields you did not name. `-c` selects characters. `-b` selects bytes. On `é`, which is two bytes, `-c1` can yield the character and `-b1` yields the first byte, which is not a character. The od dump in the tr lesson is the same class of bug. Know which flag you passed.

The CSV myth is the sentence "I will just cut on commas". The input `"a,b",c` has a comma inside quotes. `cut -d, -f1` returns `"a` and `-f2` returns `b"`. The quotes are ordinary bytes. There is no escape syntax. A field that contains the delimiter cannot be represented in the format cut understands. If your Android manifest or your benchmark table is actually CSV with quotes, parse it in a language that has a CSV reader. If your file is a delimiter-separated file with a contract that the delimiter never appears inside a field, cut is appropriate and fast.

`paste` reads lines from each file and writes them side by side, separated by a tab by default. `-d,` uses a comma. `-s` serializes one file: it joins the lines of that file with the delimiter. `paste -s -d,` of three lines is one line. `paste` does not match keys. If the files are not in corresponding order, you silently zip the wrong rows. `join` is the tool that matches keys, and it requires sorted input. Use paste when the alignment is "line N with line N" and you created both files.

`-z` on cut and paste uses NUL as the line delimiter. That is the filename-safe mode. It does not make cut understand CSV quotes either.

Extract a column from a GNU `sha256sum` manifest with `cut -d' ' -f1` only after you know the format uses two spaces and the names do not contain newlines. The checksum lesson shows the actual line. For names with spaces, cut on the first field is the hash and the rest is not one simple field. Prefer `--zero` manifests when names are hostile.

Build a two-column report with `paste` from two lists you generated in the same order, for example a list of object files and a list of their sizes from a loop that printed one then the other. If the lists can diverge, stop and use `join`.

## Tips and pitfalls

`cut -f` without `-d` uses tab. A comma file stays one field. The output looks like cut "did nothing".

`-f1-3` is a range. `-f1,3` is a set. The comma in the flag is not the delimiter.

`paste` of files with different line counts pads the shorter side. You do not get an error. Count lines with `wc -l` if alignment matters. Remember the missing-newline trap when you count.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`cut` and `paste` are single-pass and memory-light. They are faster than a spreadsheet and slower than a purpose-built parser only when the parser does more work, such as honoring quotes. Do not "speed up" CSV handling by switching to cut if the result is wrong. The cost of a wrong field is a bad Android versionName in a release note, not a saved millisecond. For a huge delimiter file that really is delimiter-safe, cut is appropriate and the bottleneck is reading the bytes, which a warm cache hides. The benchmark method on the benchmarks page is how you would time it. This lesson does not invent a cycles-per-byte figure.

title: join and comm
summary: join and comm require the same sort order. GNU checks by default. --nocheck-order will happily drop rows and exit 0.
text:
`join` merges lines that share a key. The default key is the first field, fields split on blanks. Both files must be sorted on the key with the same locale rules. `-t` sets a delimiter. `-1` and `-2` pick the key field on each side. `-a 1` keeps unpairable lines from file 1. `-e` fills a missing field. `-o` selects the output fields. This is a relational join only in the small sense of "sorted equijoin". It is not SQL.

GNU join checks that the input is sorted. On the unsorted file `b` then `a` joined to a sorted partner, this 9.4 build printed a joined line for `b`, wrote a diagnostic to stderr, and exited 1. You can see a plausible row and a failure in the same run. If a script discards stderr and does not check the status, it keeps the plausible row. `--nocheck-order` disables the check. The same unsorted input then exits 0 and still does not contain the row for `a`. That is a silent wrong answer. The flag is for the case where you have proved the order by some other means, not for making the error go away.

`comm` compares two sorted files line by line. Column 1 is lines only in file 1, column 2 is lines only in file 2, column 3 is lines in both. The columns are indented with tabs. A display that collapses tabs hides the structure. `cat -A` shows `^I`. `-1` suppresses column 1, so `comm -12` prints the intersection and `comm -13` prints lines only in file 2. GNU comm also checks order. An unsorted file produces a diagnostic and status 1, and it may already have printed something. Sort both files with the same `LC_ALL` before you comm them. `sort -u` if you need set semantics. comm does not unique the files for you; duplicate lines are part of the comparison.

Header lines break both tools. A header is an unsorted extra line at the top. Strip it with `tail -n +2` before sorting, or the check fails on line 1 for a boring reason.

## Recipes
