Join a two-column size table onto a two-column name table only after both are `sort -k1,1`. If the key is numeric and the other fields must keep their original order among ties, `sort -k1,1 -s`.

## Tips and pitfalls

A join key with extra spaces is a different key. `-t $'\t'` is the strict separator if the fields are tab-separated. The default blank splitting collapses runs of spaces and will glue a sentence into the wrong fields.

`comm` of files that are sorted in different locales fails the check or, if you disable it, lies. One `LC_ALL` for both sorts and the comm.

Do not pipe `comm` to `cut` on tabs without looking at `cat -A` first. The leading tabs are the column identity.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

Both tools are linear after the sort. The sort is the expensive part and it is the part with `-S`, `-T`, and `--parallel`. A join that re-sorts on every run of a build is paying N log N to avoid storing the data in order. If the producer can emit sorted output, skip the sort. `--nocheck-order` is not a performance feature you turn on to save the check. The check is cheap next to a wrong release diff. Locale collation makes the sort slower and the join correct only if both sides match. The sort benchmark measures collation cost. Use it before you claim `LC_ALL=C` is required for speed; use `LC_ALL=C` anyway when the keys are bytes.

title: tr works on bytes
summary: tr translates, deletes, and squeezes bytes from stdin. It has no filename operands. A UTF-8 character is more than one byte.
text:
`tr` reads stdin, writes stdout, and takes two sets as operands. It does not take a filename. `tr a b file` does not edit `file`. The shell must redirect. `SET1` and `SET2` are lists of bytes, ranges like `a-z`, and classes like `[:upper:]`. `tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'` uses `LC_CTYPE` to decide which bytes are uppercase. Under a UTF-8 locale the class is still not a promise that every Unicode letter maps the way a human expects. The safe mental model is: classes are whatever this libc says they are, and a code point encoded as several bytes is several inputs.

`-d` deletes bytes that appear in the set. `-s` squeezes repeats in the last set down to one. `-c` complements the set. `tr -s 'b'` of `abbac` is `abac`. `tr -d '\n'` joins lines. Those are the everyday uses, and they are the right uses when the data is ASCII or another single-byte encoding you have named.

The failure mode is `é`. The character U+00E9 is the bytes C3 A9. `tr 'é' 'e'` does not mean "replace that character with e". The set contains the bytes of the UTF-8 sequence as the shell passed them. In the capture, translating `é` to `e` produced two `e` bytes: both C3 and A9 were in the set built from the character, and each was replaced. `LC_ALL=C tr` of the same input to `X` produced two `X` bytes. `od -An -tx1` is how you see it. If you wanted a Unicode casefold, you wanted a program that decodes UTF-8. It is not `tr`, and it is not `sed` unless you are in a locale and a sed that actually do that and you have tested the code point.

NUL is a byte `tr` can handle. `tr '\0' '\n'` turns NULs into newlines. That is useful for a quick look and destructive for names that contained spaces and NULs as structure. Prefer `od` or a NUL-aware tool when the NULs were delimiters.

`tr` is not a performance trick for deleting a column. `cut` already does that with a defined field. `tr -d ','` deletes every comma, including ones you needed.

## Recipes

Normalize ASCII line endings by deleting `\r`: `tr -d '\r'`. That is the right tool for a CRLF file you are willing to turn into LF, and the wrong tool if some field was allowed to contain a CR.

Squeeze runs of spaces in a log: `tr -s ' '`. Do this only when the run is not significant. A Makefile and an aligned table care about the exact spaces.

## Tips and pitfalls

Ranges `A-z` are not "letters". In ASCII they include the characters between `Z` and `a`. Name the ranges you mean, or use a class and then test it.

`tr` complements with `-c` include almost everything, and the newline's fate surprises people who then join the whole file. Try the command on three lines before you run it on a tree.

Quoting the sets matters. An unquoted `*` in a set is a glob.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`tr` is a tight byte loop and it is fast relative to a shell loop that reads one character at a time. It is not faster than `cut` at a job cut defines, and it is the wrong place to look for a speedup if the program behind the pipe is `gzip` or a compiler. Locale classes can make the loop consult the locale tables. For ASCII deletion, `LC_ALL=C` makes the classification byte-simple. Measure before you export it globally; the correctness reason to use `C` is if you want byte identity, and the speed reason is the same shape as the sort locale benchmark: a heavier classification costs more per byte and may still be invisible on a small file in a warm cache.

title: sort, keys, and external merge
summary: sort compares keys, then the whole line unless -s. It spills runs to -T when the initial buffer is not enough. --parallel is a cap, not a promise.
text:
`sort` compares records. The default record ends at newline, and the newline is not part of the key. If the file does not end in a newline, GNU sort silently supplies one for the comparison. A key is a field range. Fields start at 1. The default field separator is the transition from non-blank to blank, and the blanks stay attached to the following field unless `-b` or `-t` says otherwise. `-k2,2` is "field 2 only". `-k2` is "from field 2 to the end of the line", which still includes the rest of the line in the key. Those are different sorts. `--debug` underlines the portion it used and warns about locale numeric punctuation. The underline goes to stdout with the line. The warnings go to stderr.

When all keys compare equal, sort compares the whole line as a last resort, ignoring the key options except `-r`. That last resort breaks stability: two lines with the same key can swap because the rest of the line differs. `-s` disables the last resort and keeps the input order of ties. `-u` also disables it, and it keeps one line from each equal-key group. `sort -u` and `sort | uniq` match only for the simple whole-line case. `sort -n -u` decides uniqueness on the numeric key. `sort -n | uniq` decides uniqueness on the whole line after the numeric sort. The manual states that difference. The uniq lesson shows an adjacent-line tool that cannot see a duplicate which is not adjacent.

External sort is the mechanism for inputs that do not fit in the initial buffer. Sort writes sorted runs to temporary files and merges them. `-T` selects the directory, overriding `TMPDIR`. `-S` sets the initial main-memory buffer. The manual says a bare number is in units of 1024 bytes, `%` means a percentage of physical memory, `K` multiplies by 1024, `M` by 1,048,576, and `b` means bytes. The buffer can still grow to hold a line longer than `-S`. `--compress-program` compresses the runs; the program must compress stdin to stdout and decompress with `-d`. `--parallel=N` is the number of concurrent sorts, defaulting as the manual describes, not "use every core you can find" beyond 8. None of these flags change the result if the comparison rules stay the same. They change resource use. The benchmarks measure a few of them and refuse to rank variants whose medians sit inside the noise.

`-c` checks order and exits 1 at the first disorder, with a diagnostic. `-C` is the quiet check. Status 2 is a real error, such as a missing file. `-m` merges files that are already individually sorted. Merging is faster when the premise holds, and wrong when it does not. `-z` uses NUL records so names can contain newlines.

Version sort `-V` treats digit runs as numbers, so `a2` precedes `a10`. It is not numeric sort of the whole line, and the manual has a whole chapter on where it disagrees with human "natural" expectations and with Debian version comparison. Use it for version-shaped tokens you have tested, not as a synonym for `-n`.

For a table, write the key flags on the command, not in the environment. `sort -t, -k1,1 -k2,2n` is a comma key and a numeric second key. `--debug` once when the result looks wrong, then remove it so the underlines do not enter the artifact.

Point `-T` at a directory on a filesystem with room. A sort that spills to a small tmpfs fails late. The benchmark uses the work directory and says so.

## Tips and pitfalls

`-S 1` is not "one byte". Read the unit rules before you pick a number. The examples use `1K`, which is explicit.

`--parallel` on a tiny file spends more time starting threads than comparing keys. The parallel benchmark uses 120000 lines and only compares 1 versus 2. Read its note.

title: uniq only sees neighbors
summary: uniq collapses adjacent equal lines. It does not search the file. sort makes the equals adjacent, and the locale decides what equal means.
text:
`uniq` walks the file once and compares each line to the previous line. If you hand it `a`, `b`, `a`, the two `a` lines are not adjacent, so `-d` prints nothing and the default output keeps both `a` lines with `b` between them. Sort first if "unique in the whole file" is what you meant. The sort has to use the same notion of equality. `LC_ALL=C sort` then `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 uniq` can fail to merge lines the first command separated, or merge lines it should not, depending on the bytes. Put the same `LC_ALL` on both.

`-c` prefixes a count of the adjacent run. `-d` prints one copy of lines that were repeated. `-u` prints lines that occurred once. `-D` prints all lines that were part of a repeated run. `-i` folds case for the comparison. After `LC_ALL=C sort` of `A` then `a`, `uniq -i` keeps `A`, the first of the run, because C order put `A` first and `-i` then called them equal. The survivor is the first line, not the lowercase one. If you needed the lowercase survivor, transform case before you uniq, and accept that `tr` is the wrong transform for non-ASCII.

`-f` skips fields and `-s` skips characters before comparing. `-w` limits the compare to N characters. Those options do not reorder the file. They only change which adjacent lines count as equal. If the file is not grouped by that key, the result is still wrong.

`sort -u` unique-sorts by the sort key and suppresses the last-resort compare. `sort | uniq` unique-sorts whole lines. For a two-field line where only the first field should define identity, `sort -k1,1 -u` is the operation and `uniq` is not, unless you cut the key out first. The manual's warning is the one to remember before you "simplify" a pipeline.

`-z` compares NUL-terminated records. Use it with `sort -z` on file names. A newline-uniq of a NUL stream does not see the record boundaries you created.

## Recipes

Count events in a log: `cut` the event field if it is delimiter-safe, `sort`, `uniq -c`, `sort -nr` to put the heavy counts first. The second sort is numeric on the count uniq printed. `LC_ALL=C` if the event ids are bytes.

For a set of package names, `sort -u` is enough and uniq is an extra process. Use uniq when you need the count or the `-d`/`-u` split.

## Tips and pitfalls

`uniq` without sort is valid when the producer already grouped rows, for example a database export that was ordered. Say that in the script. A future producer that changes order will silently break the report.

`-i` is not Unicode casefold. It uses the locale's case mapping on the bytes uniq compares. Test non-ASCII before you depend on it. The tr lesson showed how byte tools treat `é`.

The count format is space-padded. `cut` on that line is fragile. `awk` (not coreutils, and on this host it is mawk) is the usual field splitter. If you stay in coreutils, keep the count as the sort key and do not re-cut it unless you have frozen the format.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`uniq` is linear and cheap. The sort in front of it is the cost. A pipeline `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` sorts twice. If you only needed the counts and not a ranked list, stop after uniq. `sort -u` is one process instead of two for the simple unique case, and it can be faster because it never writes the duplicate lines to a pipe. It is not faster when you needed the counts, because it throws the multiplicity away. Do not replace `uniq -c` with `sort -u` to "speed up" a frequency report. You get a different answer. Large sorts spill, as the sort lesson described. uniq itself does not spill; it only needs the previous line.

title: shuf, random sources, and tsort
summary: shuf has no --seed. Reproducible draws come from --random-source. sort -R hashes keys. tsort orders a dependency graph.
text:
`shuf` writes a permutation of its input, or of an integer range with `-i`. `-n` stops after N lines. `-r` repeats, which can generate duplicates and will run forever if you forget `-n`. The permutation is not a sort. Equal lines stay equal as values; their positions change.

GNU shuf does not accept `--seed`. Scripts that pass it fail. The manual's random-source node describes `--random-source=FILE`: the file supplies the bytes that drive the choice. The same file and the same input produce the same permutation. `/dev/zero` is a deterministic source of zero bytes and is enough to show repeatability in a lesson. It is a poor source for a statistical sample because it is not random. For a real sample, use the kernel's generator and accept that the run will not match next time, or store the source file next to the result if you must reproduce a bug. The benchmark seed in this course is for Python's `random.Random`, which is a different generator. Do not conflate it with shuf.

`sort -R` assigns a random hash to each key and sorts the hashes. Lines with the same key stay together. `--random-source` fixes the hash function the same way. It is not a shuffle of identical keys. Use shuf when every line is an independent item. Use `sort -R` when you need grouping. Neither is a cryptographic shuffle, and neither belongs in a secret-splitting scheme.

`tsort` reads pairs and prints a topological order. Input `a b` means `a` precedes `b`. A cycle is an error. It is the coreutils tool for "compile these in an order that respects edges" when you already have a pair list. It is not `make`, and it does not read a `Cargo.toml`. A small graph is a good test of a build-system idea. A large graph with cycles needs the diagnostic, not a forced order.

`ptx` builds a permuted index. It is in the reference. It is not part of the sampling path. Mentioning it here keeps it from being mistaken for `shuf`.

### A dependency order

 


## Recipes

Pick three tests out of a list in CI when you need a short run, and check in the `--random-source` file if a failure must be reproducible. Otherwise record the chosen names in the log so the next run can repeat them without reconstructing the RNG.

Order a handful of build steps expressed as pairs with `tsort` when you are prototyping and do not want a full make graph yet. Move to a real build tool when the graph grows.

## Tips and pitfalls

`shuf file -n 2` reads the whole file. It is not a constant-memory sample of a multi-gigabyte line file. If you need a reservoir sample of a huge log, write it in the language that owns the log, or accept the memory cost knowingly.

`/dev/zero` as a random source makes the lesson deterministic and makes a statistical test meaningless. Do not publish a distribution you drew from zeros.

`tsort` on a cycle exits non-zero and prints a diagnostic. Feed it a cycle only when you are testing the failure.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`shuf` reads the whole input to permute it. Memory grows with the file. That is the limit to plan for, not CPU. `-n` does not save the read of a named file in the simple implementation you should assume; check `--help` and test a large file before you promise a streaming sample. `sort -R` is a full sort plus hashing, so it has the same spill behavior as sort. `--random-source` adds reads of the source file and does not change the big-O of the sort. `tsort` is for graphs that fit in memory. A dependency graph of a large monorepo belongs in a build tool that can persist it. None of these tools are cheaper than "do not shuffle the corpus on every test run". Shuffle once, record the sample, and reuse the names.

title: Checksums and manifests
summary: sha256sum is the usual manifest tool. md5sum is a legacy check. cksum's default is still a CRC and a byte count. A faster digest is not a better one.
text:
A checksum tool reads bytes and writes a digest. `sha256sum` is the coreutils program to put in a download page or a firmware manifest. The digest of the three bytes `abc` (no newline) is `ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad`. The example prints that line. If you include a newline in the file, you are hashing different bytes and the digest must change. `printf 'abc'` and `printf 'abc\n'` are not the same input.

`--check` reads a manifest and recomputes. A match prints `OK` unless `--status` or `--quiet` suppresses it. A mismatch prints `FAILED`, a warning, and status 1. `--status` is what a script wants, because the exit status is the result and stdout stays empty. The manifest format is part of the contract. A line that is not a digest line at all produces "no properly formatted checksum lines found" rather than FAILED. Two spaces versus a space-star (text versus binary marker) matters. When you generate and check with the same tool, you stay inside the format.

`md5sum` has the same interface and a broken collision story. Use it to verify an old file that was published with an MD5. Do not choose it for a new artifact. `sha1sum` is in the same category for new designs: SHA-1 collisions are practical. `sha224sum`, `sha384sum`, and `sha512sum` are the other SHA-2 lengths. Pick the one the protocol names.

`b2sum` is BLAKE2b. `cksum` without `-a` prints the historical POSIX CRC and the byte count, not a cryptographic digest. `cksum -a sha256 --tag` prints a BSD-style tagged line. `cksum -a` also selects md5, sha1, the SHA-2 family, blake2b, sm3, and the old `sum` algorithms. `sum -r` and `sum -s` are the legacy BSD and System V checksums. They are not interchangeable with each other or with SHA-256. `md5sum.textutils` on this system is a symlink to `md5sum`, not a second algorithm.

The checksum benchmark times md5sum, sha256sum, and b2sum on one 8 MiB warm file. A lower median does not promote that algorithm. The note on the benchmark page says this explicitly.

## Worked examples

### The abc test vector

 


### A good check and a bad hash

 


### CRC versus a tagged SHA-256

 


### Legacy sum is a different number

 


## Recipes

In a release job, hash the bytes you ship: `sha256sum --binary` or the default text mode, consistently, and store the manifest next to the artifact. Verify in CI with `sha256sum --status -c manifest`. For names that contain newlines, generate with `--zero` and check with the matching flag. Do not `cut` a zero-terminated manifest as if it were lines.

Android APK and Rust crate files are just bytes. The hash does not know they are zip archives. If you need a hash of the uncompressed contents, unpack first with a tool that understands the format (`tar` or an unzip, neither of which is coreutils) and then hash.

## Tips and pitfalls

Hashing `abc\n` because you used `echo abc` is the usual test-vector miss. The shell lesson and the printf lesson exist so the bytes are the bytes you named.

`--tag` output and the default two-space output are both checkable by the same family when the line is well formed. Mixing a macOS `shasum` line into `sha256sum -c` fails the format check. Translate deliberately, do not "fix" it by ignoring status.

`cksum` of a file and `wc -c` answer different questions. The CRC line includes a size. It is not SHA-256 shortened.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

Hash throughput is CPU and how the bytes get to the CPU. A warm page cache, which is what the benchmark uses, measures the hash and the read from RAM. A cold disk measures the disk. Reporting one number as "sha256sum's speed" without saying which is a category error. md5sum doing less cryptographic work can finish sooner and still be the wrong choice. b2sum can be faster than sha256sum on some CPUs and slower on others. The sample run on the benchmark page is one machine. Use it to learn the method, then rerun the script on the machine that will do the work if the number matters. P

title: base64, base32, and basenc
summary: These tools transform bytes into ASCII and back. They do not encrypt. GNU base64 wraps columns unless -w 0. basenc 9.4 has no base58.
text:
Encoding is a reversible spelling of bytes. Encryption is a different operation that needs a key. `base64` of a token is still the token, readable to anyone who decodes it. Use it so a binary blob can sit in a text file or a header. Do not use it as a secrecy mechanism.

GNU `base64` wraps at 76 columns by default. `-w 0` emits one line, which is what you want in a JSON string or a shell variable. `-d` decodes. `-i` ignores garbage characters such as whitespace inside the input. Without `-i`, a wrapped or spaced payload can fail the decoder depending on where the extra characters sit. The example decodes `aGVs bG8=` with `-i` back to `hello`.

`base32` is the RFC 4648 alphabet, used where the result must be case-insensitive. `-w 0` matters there too. `basenc` is the multi-alphabet tool. `--base64url` uses the URL-safe alphabet. `--z85` is the ZeroMQ alphabet and requires an input length that is a multiple of 4 for encoding. `printf 'hell'` works. `printf 'hello'` is five bytes and `basenc --z85` rejects it. That constraint is in the tool, not in the shell.

`--base58` is not in this 9.4 `basenc`. Passing it exits non-zero and names an invalid option. Bitcoin-style base58 lives elsewhere. If a blog shows `basenc --base58` and your `--help` does not list it, you do not have that feature. Do not install a random package to follow the blog in the middle of a coreutils lesson.

Decoding a truncated payload fails. Check the status. A script that ignores a decode error will feed an empty or partial file to the next stage and then checksum the wrong bytes.

## Recipes

Embed a small binary fixture in a test by storing the `base64 -w 0` line next to the test and decoding it in the setup. Checksum the decoded bytes so a truncated paste fails the test.

When an HTTP API wants base64url, use `basenc --base64url` rather than `tr` of `+/` to `-_`, which is easy to get wrong on the padding. If you do transform padding, test a length that needs padding.

## Tips and pitfalls

`base64 file > file.b64` is fine. `base64 file > file` destroys the input because the shell truncates the destination first. Same rule as `cat`.

z85's length rule is on the raw bytes for encoding. A failed z85 of `hello` is not a broken install.

`base32` output uses a different alphabet. Feeding it to `base64 -d` fails. Name the decoder that matches the encoder.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

Encoding expands data by a constant factor and is limited by memory bandwidth on large files. It is not the slow part of a build next to compression or a hash you also compute. Decoding a huge blob into a temporary file costs the write. Doing it in a shell loop per line of a multi-megabyte manifest costs a process per line, which dominates. One `base64 -d` of a concatenated payload is the coreutils-shaped solution. A language library is the right solution when you already hold the bytes in a Rust buffer and do not want to spawn a process. There is no secret faster alphabet. base64url is not quicker than base64 in any way that matters. It exists so the text survives a URL.

title: Looking at bytes with od
summary: od dumps bytes in hex, characters, or named ASCII. It is the tool you open when cat -A or a text editor has already lied.
text:
`od` reads bytes and prints them in a chosen representation. It does not modify the file. `-t x1` is hex, one byte at a time. `-t c` is the character view, with escapes for newline and similar. You can stack them: `-tx1c` prints a hex line and a character line. `-An` omits the address column so the dump is easier to compare in a test. `-w2` sets two bytes per line. The default width is wider and wraps in a way that is annoying in a narrow log.

Use `od` when any of these are in doubt: whether a newline is present, whether a UTF-8 character was split, whether a "blank" is a space or a tab or a CR, whether a NUL is in the stream. `cat -A` is a quicker visualization and it is lossy. `od` is the measurement. The fold lesson, the tr lesson, and the tac lesson all end at `od` for that reason.

`od` of a text file you think you understand is also how you learn that the editor added a newline on save. `printf 'abc' > f` followed by `od -An -tx1 f` shows `61 62 63` and nothing else. `printf 'abc\n'` adds `0a`. `wc -l` agrees with the `0a` count and disagrees with the editor's line count when the `0a` is missing. The pair of tools is the habit.

`od` will read a pipe. It has to consume the bytes to show them. It is not a pager. For a huge file, `head -c 64 | od -An -tx1` shows the prefix without dumping the rest. `tail -c` shows the suffix. That combination stays inside coreutils.

When a golden file test fails and the diff looks empty, dump both files with `od -An -tx1`. A trailing space, a CR, or a missing newline is obvious in hex and invisible in a rendered diff that trims.

When `fold` or `tr` surprises you, dump before and after. Do not argue from the terminal font.

## Tips and pitfalls

The address column changes when the file grows and makes noisy diffs. `-An` is the stable form for tests.

`-t x1z` adds a printable trailer on some versions. Stick to the format letters you have checked in `--help` for 9.4. The examples use `-tx1`, `-tx1c`, and `-ta`.

`od` prints to stdout. A redirect onto the input file truncates it first, like any other tool. Dump to a new file.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`od` formats every byte it prints, so the output is larger than the input and the CPU cost is the formatting. Dumping a multi-gigabyte core file to a terminal is the slow operation. Limit the range with `head -c` or `dd count=` first. `od` does not seek to a structure for you; `skip` via `dd` is the offset tool. There is nothing to parallelize in a 16-byte dump. The performance rule is "dump less", not "find a faster od flag".

title: du and df
summary: du walks a tree and sums allocation. df asks the filesystem how full it is. Sparse files and hard links make those numbers diverge on purpose.
text:
`du` walks directory entries, stats each file, and adds up space. By default it reports allocated space, in units that depend on the environment and the flags. This course passes `-B1` when it wants bytes of allocation, and `-b` when it wants apparent size. `-b` is defined as `--apparent-size --block-size=1`. Apparent size is the logical length, `%s` from stat. Allocated size counts blocks the filesystem has given the file, and it is smaller for a hole and larger when a short file still occupies a whole block.

A directory's own `stat` size is not the tree. The directories lesson showed a directory size that ignored `hello\n` inside. `du -s` is the sum. `-d 1` limits depth so you see children without the whole walk printed. `--exclude` skips a pattern. `-x` stays on one filesystem, which matters when a tree contains another mount. Hard links are counted once unless `-l` / `--count-links` is set. Two names for one inode are not two copies of the bytes. The links lesson created the inode; this lesson is where the accounting shows up.

`df` does not walk your tree. It calls the filesystem for free space and inode counts. A deleted file that is still open does not appear in `du` of the directory and still occupies space in `df` until the last descriptor closes. That is the resolution of "du says I freed it and df disagrees". `df -h` is human units. `df -i` is inodes. Running out of inodes looks like a full disk and is not fixed by deleting one large file.

`df --output=source,fstype,target` prints the type without `-T`. Combining `-T` and `--output` is an error on this GNU df. `stat -f -c '%T'` on the same directory can print `ext2/ext3` while df prints `ext4`, because the kernel statfs magic is shared. Trust df's fstype column for the name a person means. Trust statfs numbers for block size. The method page records both strings from the capture host.

## Worked examples

### Apparent versus allocated in a tiny tree

 


### A sparse file

 


### Hard links

 


### df and the type-code quirk

 


## Recipes

Before you delete a build tree to free a laptop, `du -h -d 1` the parent and look at which child dominates. `du -h -d 1 target` in a Rust workspace is the usual discovery that `target` is the cost. Then delete the child, then `df -h` the filesystem if you need to know whether the space came back. If a process still has files open, `df` will not move until those descriptors close. Finding the process is `lsof` or `/proc`, which are not coreutils.

`du -x` on a backup source so a mounted remote filesystem is not walked. `df -x tmpfs` to skip memory filesystems when you are looking at disks. `-x` on df is exclude-by-type, which is the GNU meaning.

## Tips and pitfalls

`du` of a file you cannot stat prints a diagnostic and continues. The total is then incomplete. Check the status.

Human units from `du -h` are not a stable sort key as text. `sort -h` knows how to order them. The sort manual describes `-h`. Prefer `-B1` and `sort -n` when you can keep the raw number.

`df` percentages are the filesystem's, including reserved blocks. A non-root user can see "space left" in the number and still get ENOSPC because of root reserve. `df` is not a quota tool.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`du` is a walk: one stat per file, and directory reads. On a tree of a million small files the metadata reads dominate and the file contents are never touched. That is why `du` can be slow on a cold cache and cheap on a warm one, and why it does not tell you read bandwidth of the file bodies. `df` is a constant-time statfs and is the tool to ask "is the disk full" without walking. Neither tool drops caches. A benchmark that runs `du` twice and reports the second run as the speed of the disk is measuring the page cache. Say so. Apparent-size mode still stats every file; it does not skip the walk. The only saving is arithmetic, not IO.

title: date and sleep
summary: GNU date -d parses a date string and @epoch. sleep accepts a decimal and a suffix. Neither one is a scheduler.
text:
`date` formats the clock or a timestamp you name. The default is "now", which makes a captured lesson unreproducible, so the examples pass `-d` or `@epoch`. `-u` forces UTC. `date -u -d @1700000000 '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ'` is a fixed instant, the same on every machine that agrees on UTC and on GNU date's parser. `date -d '2020-01-02 + 1 day'` adds a day in the parser's relative grammar. The date-input-formats node is the long description of what those strings allow. `--debug` prints how a string was interpreted. Use it when a build's `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` formatting looks shifted by a day, which is usually a timezone, not a broken calendar.

`--resolution` prints the clock resolution date believes it has. On this capture host it is one nanosecond. That is not a promise that every filesystem timestamp has nanosecond granularity, and it is not a promise that `sleep` can delay for one nanosecond accurately. It is a property of the clock interface on this kernel.

`sleep` pauses the process. `sleep 0.05` returns quickly. `sleep 1m` is a minute. `sleep foo` exits non-zero and prints "invalid time interval". Sleep is not a timer you share across machines with better than "about this long" accuracy, and it is not the tool that kills a hung child. `timeout` does that. A test that `sleep 5` to "wait for the server" is a race. Poll the condition, and use timeout as a backstop.

Do not embed `date` with no argument in a file you will checksum. The digest will change every second. Format a fixed input, or accept that the line is a label and not a byte-stable artifact.

## Worked examples

### A fixed instant

 


### A relative day

 


### Resolution of this clock

 


### Valid and invalid sleep

 


## Recipes

Stamp a release note with `date -u -d "@${SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH:-0}"` only when the epoch is actually exported. If it is unset, the `:-0` fallback is the epoch, which is obvious in the output and better than silently using "now". Prefer failing the script when the variable must be set.

Pause a retry loop with `sleep 0.2` and a counted attempt, and wrap the whole loop's command in `timeout` if the command itself can hang. Sleep does not bound the command. It only delays the next try.

## Tips and pitfalls

`date -d` of an ambiguous string can pick a timezone you did not mean. Pass `-u` and a numeric offset or `Z` when the instant must be absolute. `--debug` if you are unsure.

`TZ=UTC date` and `date -u` are related and not identical in every format. The examples use `-u`.

`sleep 0` returns immediately. It is a legal interval. It is not a yield you can count on for scheduling fairness.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`date` is a formatting process. Calling it once per file in a loop of a million files dominates the loop. Format once, or format in the language that is already walking the files. `sleep` in a polling loop is a latency choice: shorter sleeps burn wakeups, longer sleeps notice the event later. Neither is "faster" in general. A busy sleep loop is not a benchmark of the CPU. The timeout and buffering benchmarks are the ones that measure a bound and a delay with a stated input. Do not put `sleep` inside a timing trial unless the delay is the thing you are measuring, and then report it as a delay, not as work.

title: seq, numfmt, and factor
summary: seq prints numbers, numfmt rescales them, and factor splits integers. Floating-point steps and SI versus IEC rounding are the traps.
text:
`seq FIRST INCREMENT LAST` prints numbers. `seq 1 3` is 1, 2, 3. `-s,` puts commas between them instead of newlines. `-w` equalizes width with leading zeros, so `seq -w 8 10` prints `08`, `09`, `10`. `-f` is a printf format. Integer sequences are the ones to trust in a loop bound. A shell `for i in $(seq 1 100)` is still a process and a word list; a C++ or Rust loop does not need seq.

Non-integer steps use floating point. The manual's floating-point node says these conversions inherit the usual rounding, overflow, and locale decimal-point rules. The example runs `seq 0 0.1 1` and counts the lines with `wc -l`. On this GNU seq 9.4 the capture is eleven lines, ending at `1.0`. That is a measured result for this binary and this step, not a theorem about every increment. Another step can miss the endpoint. If the endpoint matters, use integers (`seq 0 100` and divide in a language with a decimal type) or check the output of the exact command you ship.

`numfmt` converts numbers to and from human units. `--to=iec` uses powers of 1024. `--to=si` uses powers of 1000. `2048` is exactly `2.0K` in IEC and rounds to `2.1K` in SI because 2048/1000 = 2.048, which rounds to one decimal as 2.1. That single digit is why a dashboard that mixes the flags lies. `--from=si` parses a suffixed number back. `--field` selects a column so you can format a byte column without touching the name column. `--invalid=ignore` leaves a bad token alone and exits 0. The default is to fail. Pick the one the pipeline needs, and do not use ignore to hide corruption.

`factor 8051` prints `8051: 83 97`. `factor 17` prints `17: 17`. `factor 1` and `factor 0` print the number and no factors. It is an arbitrary-precision factorizer for a puzzle and a teaching example, not a library you link into a service, and not a timing oracle you should build.

### Integers, width, separator

 


### A decimal step, captured rather than assumed

 


### IEC versus SI

 


### Factors

 


## Recipes

Number build shards with `seq -w 1 32` so the names sort lexically and numerically the same way. Avoid `seq 0 0.1 1` as a progress marker in a shell loop. The shell is the wrong place for a float grid.

Format a `du -B1` column for a report with `numfmt --field=1 --to=iec` after you have decided the reader wants IEC. Label the column `KiB-style` or just leave the suffix numfmt prints, and do not call it MB.

## Tips and pitfalls

`seq` writes a newline after the last number unless you change the separator and forget the final newline. `seq -s, 1 3` prints `1,2,3` and a newline. Check with `od` if a consumer is strict.

`numfmt` of a blank field fails unless `--invalid` says otherwise. A header line in the file is a blank-or-text field. Strip the header with `tail -n +2` first.

`factor` of a huge integer is CPU. Do not point it at untrusted gigabyte strings in a public service. The examples use tiny inputs.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`seq` of a million numbers is a lot of text and a lot of pipe traffic if a shell reads it line by line. Generate the numbers in-process when the consumer is C++ or Rust. `numfmt` is linear and cheap; the cost of a wrong unit is a human misreading a capacity graph, which is more expensive than the process. `factor` is exponential in the size of the integer in the worst cases that matter. A small example finishes immediately and says nothing about factoring a 2048-bit number. Do not time `factor 17` and conclude anything about cryptographic sizes. This course does not include a factoring benchmark because the interesting inputs are the ones you should not casually run, and the small ones are noise.

title: printf, echo, and yes
summary: printf is the coreutils formatter you can trust. echo is a bash builtin first and a coreutils binary second. yes repeats a line until the pipe closes.
text:
`/usr/bin/printf` formats arguments and writes bytes. `printf '%s\n' 'a b'` prints the string and a newline. `printf '%04d\n' 7` prints `0007`. The format is data, not a command. A user-supplied format string is an injection bug in any language, including this one. Keep the format literal.

Bash also has a `printf` builtin. For the format strings in this course the two agree. The lesson still writes the absolute path so the captured command is the coreutils binary and not "whatever the shell provides". `type printf` and `type /usr/bin/printf` make the distinction visible.

`echo` is the tool people reach for and the tool that then surprises them. In this bash, `echo` is a builtin. `echo --help` prints the four characters `--help` and a newline. It does not open the manual. `/usr/bin/echo --help` prints the GNU help text. `/usr/bin/echo -e 'a\tb'` interprets escapes when you pass `-e`. The default is not to interpret them (`-E`). BSD echo often interprets escapes by default. A script that depends on either behavior is already a portability bug. Use printf.

`yes` prints a line forever. `yes | head -n 2` prints `y` twice and then `yes` receives SIGPIPE because `head` closed the pipe. With `set -o pipefail`, that pipeline's status is 141 (128 + SIGPIPE). Without pipefail, the status is the status of `head`, which is 0, and the SIGPIPE is hidden. The quoting lesson introduced pipefail. This is the command that makes it visible. Do not use `yes` to fill a disk. Bound it with `head` or `timeout`.

Write generated source headers with `/usr/bin/printf`. A version banner, a `#include` guard, a Rust `const` array of bytes: the format is the contract. `echo` in that job will eventually interpret a backslash in a path.

Answer a prompt that only accepts `y` with `yes | command` only when you also bound the time. A command that stops reading still leaves `yes` writing until it dies of SIGPIPE, which is fine. A command that keeps reading fills a log. Prefer a flag on the command (`rm -f`, `apt-get -y`) over `yes`.

## Tips and pitfalls

`printf '%d' "$n"` without `\n` leaves the cursor mid-line and concatenates with the next prompt. The examples include `\n` unless the point is the missing newline.

`yes` with an argument repeats that argument. `yes n` is how you feed "no" to a prompt. It is still unbounded.

`echo -n` to suppress the newline is the non-portable form. `printf '%s' "$text"` is the portable one.

## Exercises

 


 


 


## Performance

`printf` once per record in a shell loop is process overhead if you call `/usr/bin/printf` each time, and builtin overhead if you do not. A million iterations of either is slower than formatting in the program that owns the data. `yes` is a tight write loop. It will saturate a pipe and then block. It is a useful producer in a buffering demo and a poor way to generate a test file: `dd` or `head -c` from `/dev/zero` states the size. `yes | head` measures nothing about disk. The SIGPIPE is the interesting cost: the writer is killed, the reader stops, and a pipeline that forgot pipefail reports success.

title: test and expr
summary: test and [ are the same coreutils program. expr evaluates an expression and uses exit status as a boolean. The shell builtins shadow both.
text:
`/usr/bin/test` evaluates an expression and exits 0 for true, 1 for false, and 2 when the expression itself is an error. It prints nothing on success. `/usr/bin/[` is the same program with a required closing `]`. The reference page for `[` uses the slug `bracket` because a directory named `[` breaks the static export. The manual node is still "test invocation".

In bash, `test` and `[` are builtins. `type test` says so. `type /usr/bin/test` names the file. The builtins are faster and they are not the bytes this course is teaching. Write the path in examples. In a script that must behave when `/bin/sh` is not bash, POSIX `test` is the contract, and the coreutils binary is a fine implementation of it.

Useful predicates: `-e` exists, `-f` regular file, `-d` directory, `-s` non-empty file, `-z` empty string, `-n` non-empty string, `=` string equal, `-eq` integer equal. Quote the operands. `test -n $name` is a syntax error when `name` is empty because the operand disappears. `test -n "$name"` is false and well-formed.

`expr` prints a result and uses status as a second channel. `expr 1 + 2` prints `3` and exits 0. `expr 1 = 2` prints `0` and exits 1. `expr 1 = 1` prints `1` and exits 0. A pipeline that checks only the printed text will treat a false comparison as the string `0`, which is easy to misread as success. Check `$?`. Shell arithmetic `$((1+2))` does not fork. Prefer it when you are in bash and the lesson is not "what does coreutils expr do".

The manual lists `expr` among the utilities whose exit status is not the plain 0-or-1 rule, because 2 means an error. `test` is on that list too.

The remove lesson's preserve-root default does not apply to `rm -rf -- "$build"` when the variable expands to something you did not intend. Test the prefix as well: a case statement that rejects empty, `/`, and paths without the expected parent.

Use `expr` when a strictly POSIX `sh` must do a match and you cannot assume bash `[[ ]]`. For everything else, the language you are already writing (C++, Rust) has the comparison.

## Tips and pitfalls

`[` without the space before `]` is a different command name. `/usr/bin/[` expects `]` as the last argument. Forgetting it is status 2.

`test` of too many arguments is an error, not a false result. Quote, and do not pass unquoted globs.

`expr` needs spaces around operators. `expr 1+2` is a string, not addition.

## Performance

Forking `/usr/bin/test` or `/usr/bin/expr` inside a per-file loop is the slow part. The predicate itself is a stat or a compare. The shell builtin `test` avoids the exec and is the right call when you are writing bash and you have already learned which binary you meant. A million stats is a million stats either way: the syscall remains. Batch the decision in one program when the loop is the product, not the lesson. `expr` on short strings is noise. `expr` with a pathological regular expression is a CPU sink. Do not pass untrusted patterns to it.

title: env, timeout, stdbuf, nice, nohup, nproc
summary: These six programs do not transform files. They change the environment, the clock, the stdio policy, the niceness, the hangup signal, or they report how many processors the scheduler will give you.
text:
`env` is how you exec a program with a different environment without editing the parent shell. `-C` changes the working directory for that child only. `-u NAME` removes one variable. `-i` starts from an empty environment, which is the right way to prove a build does not depend on a stray `CFLAGS` from your prompt. You must then pass `PATH` if the child needs to find binaries. `-S` splits a single argument into a command, which is useful in a shebang line and easy to quote wrong in a lesson, so the examples use `-C`, `-u`, and `-i` instead.

`timeout` starts a command and sends it a signal when the duration elapses. The default signal is TERM. The default status, when timeout itself decides the command ran too long, is 124. `--preserve-status` makes timeout exit with the status the signal produced. On this host `timeout --preserve-status 1 sleep 3` exits 143, which is 128 plus SIGTERM (15). That distinction matters in a test harness: 124 means "the wrapper fired", and 143 means "the child died of TERM" if you asked to preserve status. A command that finishes in time returns its own status, and timeout stays out of the way.

`stdbuf` adjusts buffering for programs that use stdio. It does this by arranging `LD_PRELOAD` of `libstdbuf.so` from the coreutils libexec directory before the child starts. `-oL` requests line buffering on stdout, which is the setting you want when a progress line should appear before the pipe fills. `-iL` is rejected: the manual and the binary agree that line buffering stdin is meaningless, and the status is 125, one of the special statuses the exit-status node lists for `stdbuf`. `cat` and `dd` are called out in the manual because they do not use stdio for the data path, so stdbuf does not change their block size. `tee` resets buffering on its own. The buffering benchmark in this course measures a program that does use stdio, and it reports the numbers it measured. It does not claim a universal speedup.

`nice` adds to the niceness of a command. A positive adjustment makes the process more willing to yield. On this host `nice -n 5 true` exits 0. A negative adjustment asks to be less nice, which an ordinary user cannot do. `nice -n -1 true` prints "cannot set niceness: Permission denied" and still runs the command. The status is the command's status, so `true` yields 0 and `false` yields 1. The warning is not a failed command unless you treat stderr as fatal. Do not wrap `nice` around a benchmark and then claim the elapsed time changed because of the warning. This course does not rank nice levels.

`nohup` arranges for the child to ignore SIGHUP and, if stdout is a terminal, redirects it to `nohup.out`. When stdout is already redirected, `nohup` does not create that file. The example redirects to `redirected.out` and lists the directory so you can see the absence. `nohup` is not a service manager. A child that ignores hangup still dies when the machine reboots, and it still needs `timeout` if it can hang.

`nproc` prints how many processors are available to the current process, after considering affinity and cgroup limits the kernel reports. `--all` prints the installed count. `--ignore=N` subtracts N, which is the usual way to leave one processor for the desktop while a compile runs. On the capture host the three numbers were 4, 4, and 3 in the order `nproc`, `nproc --all`, `nproc --ignore=1`. Your laptop can differ. Use the value as a starting `-j` for a build. It is not a measurement of memory bandwidth, and a machine with 4 processors and 2 GiB of RAM will thrash if every job is a linking C++ binary. The performance lesson and the benchmark page are where resource tradeoffs are stated with inputs attached.

title: tee, mktemp, pathchk, and mkfifo
summary: tee splits a stream without rereading it. mktemp makes an unguessable scratch name. pathchk rejects names that will not travel. mkfifo is a pipe with a filesystem entry.
text:
`tee` reads stdin once and writes the same bytes to stdout and to every file you name. That is how you keep a log of a pipeline without running the producer twice. `printf 'ab\n' | tee a.txt b.txt` creates two files of three bytes and also writes those three bytes to stdout. `-a` appends. Without `-a`, tee truncates each file at the start, the same way a shell redirect does. The order of writes to the files and to stdout is not a transaction: a full disk on the second file can leave the first file complete and the pipeline failing. Check the status.

The manual notes that `tee` is one of the programs that resets its own buffering. Putting `stdbuf` in front of `tee` does not give you a free line-buffered split. If you need a line to appear in a log before a later stage finishes, look at the producer, not at a second stdbuf wrapped around tee.

`mktemp` creates a file or, with `-d`, a directory, using a template that ends in at least six `X` characters. It replaces the `X`s with random characters and creates the object with `O_EXCL`, so two racing scripts do not share the name. The course runner already gives every example a private directory. You still want `mktemp` inside a script that a person will run on their own machine, because `/tmp/out` is a shared name and a symlink attack. Print the name mktemp prints. Do not invent a parallel "random" name with `date` alone. The clock is a poor unique id when two jobs start in the same second.

`pathchk` answers a different question: would this name be legal and portable? `-p` checks the POSIX portable filename character set. A newline fails. `pathchk` does not create the file and does not look at whether you have permission. It is the check you run on a name you are about to embed in a release tarball, not a substitute for `mkdir`.

`mkfifo` creates a named pipe. Opening it for reading blocks until a writer opens it, and the reverse. `timeout 1 cat fifo` with no writer exits 124. That is the same timeout status as the process-wrapper lesson, applied to a pipe that nobody is writing. Named pipes are useful in a demo of "this command waits" and a poor place to store data. A fifo has a name and no contents you can `ls` the size of in a useful way. The size stays zero. The bytes exist only while a reader and a writer are both connected.

Record a long build log and still watch it with `command 2>&1 | tee build.log`. The shell redirect applies to the whole pipeline's display. tee is what copies the bytes into the file. Add `-a` only when you mean to continue yesterday's log.

Create a work directory with `work=$(mktemp -d)` and remove it in an `EXIT` trap. Put intermediates there. A fixed path in `$HOME` collides with the previous run and survives a crash in a way that hides bugs.

Run `pathchk -p` on every filename a code generator emits before you write the file. A C++ header named with a space will build on your laptop and fail in a tool that splits on whitespace. Fail the generator.

## Tips and pitfalls

`mktemp` with a template that does not end in `XXXXXX` fails. Six `X` characters is the minimum. A template in a directory you cannot write also fails. The status is non-zero and no name is printed.

`tee` of a file you are also reading is a classic truncation bug. `tee file < file` empties the file. Write to a new name and `mv` it.

`pathchk` accepting a name does not mean the filesystem will accept it. A too-long UTF-8 name can pass a character-set check and still fail in `open`. `pathchk` without `-p` also checks length against the filesystem. Use both checks when the name is destined for this machine and for a tarball.

A fifo left in a directory looks like a file. `rm` removes the name. Do not `cp` a fifo and expect bytes. There are no stored bytes.

title: Identity, the host, and what is not a terminal
summary: id, whoami, uname, and hostid describe the account and the kernel. users, who, logname, and tty describe a login session this capture does not have. SELinux tools fail closed here.
text:
`id` prints the user and group identifiers of the process. `id -un` prints the name only. `whoami` prints that same name. On this capture both print the sandbox account, which is the account the runner used, not a student name and not a machine name. `groups` lists the supplementary groups. Those groups are why a process can read plugdev or sudo-owned files. They are not a list of logged-in people.

`uname -srm` prints the kernel name, the release, and the machine. This host produced a line beginning `Linux` and ending `x86_64`. The lesson uses `-srm` on purpose. `-n` would print the nodename, and a nodename is often a hostname you did not mean to publish in a course page or a bug report. `arch` prints the machine hardware name and matches the trailing field of that `uname` line on this host. Neither command reads `/etc/hostname`. The `hostname` binary on Ubuntu is a different package, documented with the companions.

`users` and `who` read the login accounting files. In this capture there is no logged-in user in that table. `users` prints nothing and exits 0. `who` prints nothing and exits 0. An empty success is not "the command is broken". It is "the table is empty". `pinky` prints a header and no rows in the same situation. `logname` asks for the login name associated with the terminal and fails here with "no login name", status 1. `tty` prints "not a tty" and exits 1, because the runner's stdout is a pipe, not a terminal. The exit-status node lists `tty` as a command whose non-zero status is an answer. A script that does `set -e` and then calls `tty` will stop on a pipe, which is often what you want when you were about to launch an interactive pager.

`hostid` prints a 32-bit hex identifier. The captured value on this host is `007f0100`. Treat it as a host tag the binary printed, not as a credential and not as proof of a particular network address. Do not key a license check on it. It is stable enough to confuse you and weak enough to be the wrong authenticator.

`printenv` prints the environment. It is the inspection tool that matches `env`, which modifies the environment for a child. `printenv HOME` prints the sandbox home the runner set. `printenv` of an unset name exits 1. That status is one of the exceptions in the exit-status node.

SELinux is not enabled on this kernel. `id -Z` exits 1 and says `--context` works only on an SELinux-enabled kernel. `chcon` cannot apply a partial context to an unlabeled file. `runcon` exits 125 and says it may be used only on an SELinux kernel. The course records those failures so you do not copy a Fedora snippet onto this Ubuntu image and treat the failure as a mystery. `stty` is installed and is the tool that changes terminal settings. The examples do not run it against a terminal. `--help` is as far as this lesson goes, because a stray `stty` in a captured session can change echo and erase for the person watching.

title: Mechanisms that decide speed
summary: Locale collation, stdio buffering, external sort, sparse files, and reflink decide cost. This lesson shows the mechanisms with captured behavior and points at the benchmark page for numbers.
text:
Speed in coreutils is a property of a bottleneck, not a property of a flag you can memorize as "the fast one". The same `sort` is cheap on a thousand integers and expensive when it spills. The same `cp` is a metadata operation when the filesystem can share extents, and a full read-write when it cannot. The same `wc -l` is a streaming scan that never builds a line list. This lesson fixes the mechanisms. The benchmark page is where a fixed input, a seed, five trials, and a median are recorded, with the version, the filesystem, and the warm-cache limit written next to the numbers. If a gap there is smaller than the spread of the trials, the page says not to rank the variants. This lesson does not add a second, quieter ranking.

Collation is the first mechanism people trip over. `LC_ALL=C` compares bytes. `en_US.UTF-8` groups case and applies the locale's weights, so the same four letters come out in a different order. The work is not "more flags". The work is a heavier comparison function, called once per pair the algorithm needs, and it cannot be skipped by `-S` or `--parallel`. Those flags change memory and thread count for the external merge. They do not switch the comparator. `sort -S` sets the main buffer. The manual's unit rules are picky: a bare number is 1024-byte units, `K` is 1024, `M` is 1048576, `%` is a percent of memory. The buffer can still grow to hold a long line. `-T` chooses the spill directory and overrides `TMPDIR`. `--parallel` defaults to the available processors and is capped at 8, and the manual warns that the merge wants memory that grows with the thread count. `--compress-program` must compress stdin to stdout and decompress with `-d`. All of that is in the sort lesson with a captured spill log. The benchmark page repeats the comparison on a fixed input and reports medians. A single interactive run is not that page.

Buffering is the second mechanism. A program that uses stdio and writes to a pipe uses a large block buffer by default. The reader sees nothing until the block fills or the writer exits. `stdbuf -oL` requests a line buffer by preloading `libstdbuf.so`. It does not apply to `cat` and `dd`, which do not use stdio for their data, and `tee` resets its own buffering. The latency you care about in a progress pipe is time-to-first-byte. The throughput you care about in a checksum is bytes per second of the hash, and line buffering can make that worse by issuing more writes. The buffering benchmark records a first-byte delay. Read it as a delay, not as a claim that line buffering is faster.

`wc` is the model of a streaming tool. `wc -l` counts newline bytes. `printf 'abc' | wc -l` is 0. `wc -c` on the same bytes is 3. `wc -m` counts characters and has to decode UTF-8, so it is the slower mode when the locale is multibyte and the file is large. The benchmark page runs `-c`, `-l`, and `-m` on one generated ASCII file so the difference is the scan, not a different input. Do not quote those medians as the cost of Unicode. The input is ASCII on purpose.

Filesystem shape is the fourth mechanism. `truncate -s 1M` creates a hole. `stat` shows a large size and zero allocated blocks on this filesystem. `du -b` reports the apparent size. `du -B1` reports the allocation, which is 0 for that fresh hole. A backup tool that reads the apparent size copies a megabyte of zeros. A tool that copies extents can keep the hole. `cp --reflink=always` on this ext4 asks for a clone and fails with "Operation not supported". `--reflink=auto` falls back to a copy and exits 0. The benchmark page compares a plain copy with `dd` on an 8 MiB file and says the filesystem up front. It does not claim reflink won, because reflink did not work here.

Caches sit under all of this. The course creates inputs and rereads them. The page cache holds the data. Nobody ran `drop_caches`, and an ordinary user cannot. A second trial is warmer than a first trial on a quiet machine and still not a cold-disk number. RSS is Linux `ru_maxrss` in ki

title: Pipelines that fail closed
summary: Spaces, newlines, empty variables, and SIGPIPE are how a short script deletes the wrong tree or reports success after a writer died. The fixes are quoting, explicit targets, and pipefail.
text:
A pipeline is safe when every name is one word, every deletion has a target you computed, and a dead writer is allowed to fail the script. Coreutils will do exactly what the shell asks after the shell has already split the words. Most "rm disasters" are word-splitting and empty variables, not a bug in `rm`.

Quoting comes first. `printf 'hello world\n' > "my file"` creates one file. The same redirect without quotes creates `my` and then tries to write `world` as a command, or worse, passes two operands to a later `rm`. The quoting lesson covers globs. This lesson is the part where you apply it to destruction. Double quotes allow expansions and prevent splitting. Single quotes prevent expansions. A name you got from a variable is always quoted: `"$path"`.

Newlines in names are legal on Linux. `ls` with the default quoting can hide them or render them as a question mark depending on version and options. `--quoting-style=shell-escape` prints a form you can tell is one name. `ls --zero` emits NUL separators so a reader does not have to parse the escape. `find -print0` and `xargs -0` are the findutils pair, not coreutils, and they are the right producer when the walk is recursive. Coreutils tools that support `-z` (`sort -z`, `uniq -z`, `comm` has related options you should read in `--help` before you assume them) keep the NUL boundary. The filename lesson is the longer treatment. The rule to remember here is: if you pipe `ls` to anything, you have already given up, unless you used `--zero` and a reader that understands it.

Deletion comes second. `rm -rf -- "$dir"` is safe only when `$dir` is the directory you created. The double dash stops a name that begins with `-` from becoming a flag. `--preserve-root` is the default, which blocks `rm -rf /` specifically. It does not block `rm -rf /tmp` or `rm -rf "$dir"` when `dir` is empty. An empty expansion of an unquoted variable vanishes. An empty expansion of a quoted variable is an empty argument, and `rm` will complain. Test the string before you call `rm`. Refuse empty. Refuse `/`. Prefer to `cd` into a parent you created and delete a relative name. The example creates `build/obj`, removes `build`, and checks that the name is gone. It does not touch the real root.

`rm -I` asks once when you pass more than three files, and with an empty stdin it removes nothing and exits 0. That status is easy to misread as "I deleted them". The remove lesson captures it. If you need a prompt, also check that the files are gone. Do not use `-I` as your only safety check.

SIGPIPE is the third failure. `yes | head -n 2` prints two lines and then `yes` is killed because `head` closed the pipe. With `set -o pipefail` the pipeline status is 141. Without it, the status is `head`'s status, which is 0, and a script reports success for a writer that died. The printf lesson shows the same pipeline. Turn pipefail on in any script whose middle stage is not allowed to fail quietly. `set -e` does not by itself give you pipefail.

title: Tools that are not coreutils
summary: find, xargs, grep, sed, awk, and tar sit beside the toolbox and are easy to misfile as coreutils. hostname, kill, and uptime are in the GNU manual and still belong to other Ubuntu packages. rsync, perf, and GNU time are not installed here.
text:
Coreutils is a bounded set. The introduction in the manual describes that set. Everything else you type in a shell is a guest. Guests are useful. Calling them coreutils leads to the wrong manual, the wrong bug tracker, and a script that assumes a flag the package never shipped. This lesson runs the guests and names the package.

`find` and `xargs` come from findutils. `find` walks a tree. `find -print0` ends each path with a NUL. `xargs -0` reads those paths and builds argument lists. Together they are the recursive form of the NUL-safe habit in the filename lesson. `xargs` has its own failure rules: by default a command that exits 255 can stop the whole run, and without `-0` it splits on blanks. A space in `my file` is the test. `wc -c` from coreutils can count the file once xargs has passed the name through intact.

`grep` searches. Coreutils does not. `grep -n` prints the line number. It is the right tool for "which line contains this token" and the wrong tool to cite as a coreutils one-liner. The remove lesson uses grep only as a companion to find a phrase in `rm --help`.

`sed` is a stream editor with its own language. `sed -n '2p'` prints the second line. `tail` and `head` can slice by count. They cannot apply an edit script. When you need the second line only, `sed -n '2p'` or `tail -n +2 | head -n 1` both work. The second form stays inside coreutils. Prefer it when the lesson is coreutils. Use sed when you are already in a sed script, and say so.

`awk` is a field language. On this host `/usr/bin/awk` is mawk, selected by the alternatives system, not GNU awk. A script that uses gawk-only features will fail here even though `awk` exists. The example prints the second field of one line and the version line mawk reports. `cut` is the coreutils field tool, and it splits on a single character. It does not evaluate an awk expression, and it does not understand CSV quotes. That limit has its own cookbook recipe.

`tar` writes a tape archive. `cp -a` copies a tree and is not an archive format. The example creates a one-file tar and lists it. Compression flags belong to tar and to gzip, not to coreutils. This course does not teach tar's format beyond "it is a different package".

`hostname`, `kill`, and `uptime` have nodes in the GNU coreutils manual because the upstream project documents them. Ubuntu packages them elsewhere. `dpkg -S` on the three paths shows the owning packages. The orientation lesson made the same point with the version of coreutils you do have. Read the manual node only after you have checked which binary answered.

`rsync` is not installed. `perf` is not installed. `/usr/bin/time` is not installed. The shell keyword `time` is bash, and it does not print maximum RSS. The benchmark helper uses Python's `resource` module for that counter and says so in the disclosure. Do not paste a GNU time format string into this environment and expect a binary to appear.

title: A small build, install, and checksum
summary: The daily path for a C++, Rust, or Android tree is install, nproc, sha256sum, and timeout. This lesson runs that path on a one-file C program and a payload manifest.
text:
A developer workstation uses coreutils in the gaps around the compiler. The compiler is not coreutils. `gcc` is not coreutils. `rustc` and `gradle` are not coreutils. The tools that place the binary, count the processors, hash the artifact, and stop a hung test are coreutils, and they are the ones a build script gets wrong when it uses `cp` and hopes.

`install -D -m 755 src/app dest/bin/app` copies the file, creates `dest/bin` if needed, and sets the mode. `-D` is the difference from `cp` followed by a separate `mkdir` and `chmod` that can race. `-m 755` is applied after the install umask handling the manual describes. The permissions lesson covers `install -C`, which preserves the mtime when the content matches, and the non-portable warning on `cp -n`. This lesson uses the plain install that a prefix expects. The mode in the capture is whatever `stat -c '%a'` prints. Read it. Do not assume a blog's `chmod` line ran.

A checksum is the artifact's identity. `sha256sum blob > MANIFEST` writes a line the same tool can check with `-c`. The check prints `OK` and exits 0 when the bytes match. A wrong digest exits non-zero. The checksum lesson shows a deliberately bad line. Here the manifest matches, because a release script that cannot round-trip a good file is not ready for a bad one. Hash the bytes you ship. Hashing a filename list without the contents does not catch a corrupt object file.

`nproc` is the starting point for `-j` in make, ninja, or cargo. `--ignore=1` leaves a processor for everything that is not the build. The number is local. The capture prints it. A linking C++ job can use more RAM than a processor count suggests, and an Android gradle build can saturate disk before it saturates CPUs. Raise the job count until RSS or the disk queue says stop. The performance lesson states that rule without a fake timing table.

`timeout` belongs around tests and around network fetches a build should not wait on forever. `timeout 2` of a program that returns immediately passes the program's status through. `timeout 1 sleep 3` returns 124. A CI script that treats every non-zero as "the compiler failed" will mis-file a hang. Branch on 124.

The shell around these tools still has the quoting rules from the previous lesson. A prefix in a variable is quoted. An empty prefix is refused. `install` will happily write to a relative `dest` you created in the scratch directory. That is the shape to copy. A script that `install`s into `/` because a variable was empty is the shape to reject before the command runs.

Rust and Android fit the same pattern even though this capture does not invoke them. `cargo build --release` writes a binary you then `install` into a prefix. An NDK archive you downloaded is a file you `sha256sum -c` against the digest the vendor published. `timeout` bounds the emulator test. None of those products are coreutils. The four commands around them are.

summary: Concatenate FILE(s) to standard output.
text: Streams files to stdout. -A shows tabs, ends, and other nonprinting bytes. The manual says cat does not use C FILE streams, so stdbuf does not change its buffering. It is the wrong tool for random access.

title: chcon
summary: Change the SELinux security context of each FILE to CONTEXT.
text: Changes an SELinux security context. This capture host has no SELinux-enabled kernel, and chcon fails on unlabeled files. Do not treat a failure here as a permissions-bit problem; chmod is a different mechanism.

title: chgrp
summary: Change the group of each FILE to GROUP.
text: Changes group ownership. Without privilege you can only move a file to a group you belong to. --reference copies the group from another file. BSD chgrp does not take GNU long options.

title: chmod
summary: Change the mode of each FILE to MODE.
text: Changes mode bits with an octal mode or a symbolic mode. --reference copies a mode. It does not change the owner. Recursive -R on a tree you do not mean to publish is the usual accident.

title: chown
summary: Change the owner and/or group of each FILE to OWNER and/or GROUP.
text: Changes user and group. On this sandbox, chown to root fails with Operation not permitted. --from avoids racing with another owner. GNU --reference is not a BSD flag.

title: cksum
summary: Print or verify checksums.
text: The historical CRC plus byte count is still the default. -a selects md5, the SHA-2 family, blake2b, sm3, and the old sum algorithms. --tag is how cryptographic digests print a BSD-style line; the CRC line stays numeric.

title: comm
summary: Compare sorted files FILE1 and FILE2 line by line.
text: Compares two sorted files line by line and prints three columns. GNU comm checks order and exits 1 when it is wrong, after it may already have written lines. Suppress columns with -1, -2, and -3.

title: cp
summary: Copy SOURCE to DEST, or multiple SOURCE(s) to DIRECTORY.
text: Copies files and trees. -a is -dR --preserve=all. --reflink=always fails on this ext4 filesystem; --reflink=auto falls back to a read/write copy. --sparse controls holes. -n is marked non-portable in 9.4; use --update=none.

title: csplit
summary: Output pieces of FILE separated by PATTERN(s) to files 'xx00', 'xx01', ...,
text: Splits a file at context lines rather than at a fixed size. Patterns are basic regular expressions. -z suppresses empty pieces. It is not a CSV or JSON parser. Stock macOS does not ship GNU csplit.

title: cut
summary: Print selected parts of lines from each FILE to standard output.
text: Selects byte, character, or field ranges. -d sets a single-byte delimiter. It does not understand quotes, so a CSV comma inside quotes is still a separator. --complement and --output-delimiter are GNU extensions.

title: date
summary: Display date and time in the given FORMAT.
text: Formats and parses dates. -d takes a date string, including @epoch. BSD date uses -v and -f instead. --debug explains a parse. The clock resolution reported by --resolution is a property of this host.

title: dd
summary: Copy a file, converting and formatting according to the operands.
text: Copies blocks. status=progress and status=none are GNU. conv=sparse seeks over NUL blocks. iflag=fullblock matters when reading a pipe that returns short reads. Never point of= at a device in an example you have not identified.

title: df
summary: Show information about the file system on which each FILE resides,
text: Reports filesystem free space from statfs, not by walking files. GNU df -T prints the type. On BSD, df -T filters by type instead. --output and -T cannot be combined. This host's df -T says ext4 where stat -f says ext2/ext3.

title: dir

text: dir is ls with a different default format, still the same coreutils binary family. Scripts should call ls with explicit options so a dir default never becomes part of the contract.

title: dircolors
summary: Output commands to set the LS_COLORS environment variable.
text: Prints shell commands that set LS_COLORS. The database is not consulted unless the shell evaluates that output. Color is a display hint. It does not change the bytes ls writes when --color=never.

title: dirname
summary: Output each NAME with its last non-slash component and trailing slashes
text: Prints everything through the last slash. Multiple operands are allowed. -z changes the output delimiter; it does not make dirname read NUL-separated stdin. A path with no slash yields '.'.

title: du
summary: Summarize device usage of the set of FILEs, recursively for directories.
text: Walks a tree and sums allocated space, counting a hard link once unless -l is set. --apparent-size or -b reports the logical size, which is what sparse files make diverge from du without that flag. df does not walk the tree.

title: echo
summary: Echo the STRING(s) to standard output.
text: The manual recommends printf for anything that must be portable. Bash's builtin echo ignores --help and prints the word. /usr/bin/echo is coreutils, and -E (no escapes) is its default. -e is a GNU behavior, not POSIX.

title: env
summary: Set each NAME to VALUE in the environment and run COMMAND.
text: Runs a command with a modified environment. -i starts empty, -u removes a name, -C changes directory, and -S splits a string for shebangs. The manual lists env among commands with special exit statuses. BSD env lacks -S.

title: expand
summary: Convert tabs in each FILE to spaces, writing to standard output.
text: Turns tabs into spaces. -t sets tab stops. -i affects only leading tabs. It does not reflow paragraphs; fmt does that. Tabs inside the data are bytes, not a table layout.

title: expr

text: Evaluates an expression and prints it. A true comparison prints 1 and exits 0. A false comparison prints 0 and exits 1. That inversion surprises people who treat the printed number as the exit status. Prefer test or shell arithmetic for new scripts.

title: factor

text: Prints prime factors of arbitrary-precision integers. factor 1 and factor 0 print the number and no factors. It is not a general cryptography library and it is not a reason to invent timing claims.

title: false

text: Exits with status 1. Bash also has a builtin false. /usr/bin/false --version identifies coreutils. The manual lists false as an ordinary failure status, unlike test's use of 1 as an answer.

title: fmt
summary: Reformat each paragraph in the FILE(s), writing to standard output.
text: Reflows paragraphs to a width. -w sets the width and -p keeps a mail-style prefix. It is not a code formatter and it will join short lines that look like a paragraph. BSD fmt exists with a different option set.

title: fold
summary: Wrap input lines in each FILE, writing to standard output.
text: Wraps lines at a width. On this UTF-8 locale, fold -w 1 split the two bytes of U+00E9. Do not assume a column width keeps a multibyte character intact; check with od. -b counts bytes. -s breaks at spaces.

title: groups

title: head
summary: Print the first 10 lines of each FILE to standard output.

title: join

title: link
summary: Call the link function to create a link named FILE2 to an existing FILE1.
text: Creates a hard link with link(2) and no extra flags. It will not replace an existing name and it will not link a directory for an unprivileged user. ln is the tool with -s, -f, and -r. unlink is the matching removal call.

title: ln

text: Makes hard and symbolic links. -s is a symlink. GNU -r / --relative rewrites the target as a relative path. -sfn retargets a symlink even when the destination name exists. BSD ln has no --relative.

title: logname
summary: Print the user's login name.
text: Prints the name from the login utmp record. In this non-login sandbox it fails. whoami reads the effective uid instead and still works. Do not use logname as a synonym for the account that owns the files.

title: ls
summary: List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
text: Lists names and, with -l, metadata. The shell expands globs before ls sees them. --quoting-style=shell-escape makes odd names visible. --zero delimits with NUL. GNU -T is tab size; BSD ls -T is a time format. dir and vdir are related entry points.

summary: Print or check MD5 (128-bit) checksums.
