title: mkdir
summary: Create the DIRECTORY(ies), if they do not already exist.
text: Creates directories. -p creates parents and does not fail if the leaf exists. -m applies to the final component created in that invocation; parents are created under the current umask, which is 0022 here, so they land at 755 when -m 700 is asked.

title: mkfifo
summary: Create named pipes (FIFOs) with the given NAMEs.
text: Creates a named pipe. Opening it blocks until the other end is opened. A lesson that reads a fifo must bound the wait with timeout, or the sandbox hangs. mkfifo does not copy bytes; the readers and writers do.

title: mknod
summary: Create the special file NAME of the given TYPE.
text: Creates fifos, and device nodes when you pass a type and numbers. Device nodes need privileges this course does not use. Prefer mkfifo for a named pipe. Do not run mknod against /dev in examples.

title: mktemp
summary: Create a temporary file or directory, safely, and print its name.
text: Creates a temporary file or directory with a unique name. The template must end in at least six X characters. -d makes a directory. --suffix appends a suffix after the X's. Leaving the default /tmp is fine; the course scripts also set TMPDIR to the sandbox.

title: mv
summary: Rename SOURCE to DEST, or move SOURCE(s) to DIRECTORY.
text: Renames, or copies and unlinks when the destination is another filesystem. -n refuses to overwrite and, on this GNU version, exits 1. -t collects sources into a directory. There is no cross-device rename system call; EXDEV is why the copy happens.

title: nice
summary: Run COMMAND with an adjusted niceness, which affects process scheduling.
text: Adjusts niceness and runs a command. The manual says a negative adjustment without privilege prints a warning and continues as if the adjustment were zero. The exit status is the command's status, not the warning. renice is a different program and is not coreutils.

title: nl
summary: Write each FILE to standard output, with line numbers added.
text: Numbers lines. -ba is -b a, which numbers every line including blanks. The default body style skips blanks. It is a formatter, not a way to address lines for editing. BSD nl differs in style names.

title: nohup
summary: Run COMMAND, ignoring hangup signals.
text: Runs a command immune to SIGHUP and, if stdout is a terminal, redirects it to nohup.out. When stdout is already redirected, nohup.out is not created. It does not daemonize, and it does not change niceness.

title: nproc
summary: Print the number of processing units available to the current process,
text: Prints the number of processing units available to the process, which can be less than --all when the affinity mask is smaller. --ignore subtracts from that count. GNU documents the default sort --parallel cap in terms of available processors. nproc is not in BSD base.

title: numfmt
summary: Reformat NUMBER(s), or the numbers from standard input if none are specified.
text: Formats numbers with SI or IEC suffixes. 2048 becomes 2.0K in IEC (1024) and 2.1K in SI (1000) because of rounding. --field selects a column. It is GNU-only. It does not change sort's numeric comparison; sort -h has its own rules.

title: od
summary: Write an unambiguous representation, octal bytes by default,
text: Dumps bytes in hex, octal, or named characters. Use it when cat -A is not enough, especially for NULs and encoding mistakes. -An drops the address. -w sets the width. hexdump is a different program and is not coreutils.

title: paste
summary: Write lines consisting of the sequentially corresponding lines from
text: Merges lines from files, or, with -s, joins lines of one file. -d sets the delimiter. -z uses NUL as the record separator. It does not sort or match keys; join does that.

title: pathchk
summary: Diagnose invalid or non-portable file names.
text: Checks whether a name is portable. -p applies the POSIX portable character set and a length limit. A name containing | fails -p. It does not create the file and it does not tell you whether the directory is writable.

title: pinky
summary: in short format
text: A lightweight who. With nobody recorded in utmp it prints a header and no rows, which is what this sandbox shows. It is GNU-specific. who reads the same kind of login records.

title: pr
summary: Paginate or columnate FILE(s) for printing.
text: Paginates and columns text. -t drops the header and footer so the output can go to another filter. -s sets a column separator. It is not a table join. Default headers include the date, so scripts that need stable bytes pass -t.

title: printenv
summary: Print the values of the specified environment VARIABLE(s).
text: Prints the environment or one variable. A missing name exits non-zero, which the manual calls out. -0 uses NUL delimiters. env runs a command; printenv only displays.

title: printf
summary: Print ARGUMENT(s) according to FORMAT, or execute according to OPTION:
text: Formats operands. Bash also has a builtin printf. Use /usr/bin/printf when you need the coreutils binary, including %q for shell quoting. The format string is not a filename. Prefer printf over echo for escapes and missing newlines.

title: ptx
summary: Output a permuted index, including context, of the words in the input files.
text: Builds a permuted index. It is a specialized text tool, not a sort replacement. The output columns are easy to misread; the manual's ptx section documents the format. Most developer workflows never need it.

title: pwd
summary: Print the full filename of the current working directory.
text: Prints the working directory. Bash's builtin pwd is what you get if you type pwd. /usr/bin/pwd is coreutils. -P resolves symlinks; -L follows the logical $PWD. The builtin and the binary agree on this sandbox because the directory is not reached through a link.

title: readlink
summary: Print value of a symbolic link or canonical file name
text: Prints the target of a symlink, or, with -f, a canonical path. -f allows the final component to be missing and still exits 0. -e requires every component to exist. GNU -f is not what older BSD readlink implemented.

title: realpath
summary: Print the resolved absolute file name;
text: Prints an absolute path. The default allows a missing final component. -e requires the path to exist. -m allows missing middle components. --relative-to prints a path relative to a base. Older macOS installs did not ship realpath.

title: rm
summary: Remove (unlink) the FILE(s).
text: Removes directory entries. GNU defaults include --preserve-root. -I prompts once before removing more than three items or descending recursively; an EOF answer left the files in place and still exited 0 in this sandbox. -i prompts per file. It does not shred data.

title: rmdir
summary: Remove the DIRECTORY(ies), if they are empty.
text: Removes empty directories. A non-empty directory and a regular file both fail, with different messages. -p removes parent components if they become empty. Use rm -r only when you mean to delete contents.

title: runcon
summary: Run a program in a different SELinux security context.
text: Runs a command in a different SELinux context. It needs a kernel with SELinux. This host does not have one. It is not a substitute for sudo and not a coreutils permission bit.

title: seq
summary: Print numbers from FIRST to LAST, in steps of INCREMENT.
text: Prints a sequence of numbers. -w equalizes width and -s sets the separator. The floating-point section of the manual applies. On 9.4, seq 0 0.1 1 prints 11 values ending at 1.0 for this particular step; that is not a proof that every step is exact.

title: sha1sum
summary: Print or check SHA1 (160-bit) checksums.
text: SHA-1 checksums, 160-bit, same interface as sha256sum. Collision attacks against SHA-1 are practical. Do not choose it for a new manifest. The manual groups it with the SHA-2 tools even though SHA-1 is not SHA-2.

title: sha224sum
summary: Print or check SHA224 (224-bit) checksums.
text: SHA-224, a truncated SHA-256 variant with a different initial state. Same -c interface. Rare in download pages. Prefer sha256sum unless a protocol names SHA-224.

title: sha256sum
summary: Print or check SHA256 (256-bit) checksums.
text: SHA-256 checksums. This is the usual coreutils tool for a download manifest. --check reads the GNU line format. A wrong hash prints FAILED and exits 1. The digest of the three bytes abc is a known test vector used in the lesson.

title: sha384sum
summary: Print or check SHA384 (384-bit) checksums.
text: SHA-384, the truncated SHA-512 variant. Same command-line shape as sha256sum. Choose it when a protocol says SHA-384, not because the name looks longer than SHA-256.

title: sha512sum
summary: Print or check SHA512 (512-bit) checksums.
text: SHA-512. The digest is longer and the implementation processes 64-bit words. On a small file the runtime difference may sit inside the noise. Use the benchmark if you need a number, and do not generalize it.

title: shred
summary: Overwrite the specified FILE(s) repeatedly, in order to make it harder
text: Overwrites a file, and -u unlinks it afterward. The manual's assumption is that the filesystem and the device overwrite in place. Journals, snapshots, compression, RAID, and SSD wear leveling break that assumption. One pass in a lesson only shows the user interface.

title: shuf
summary: Write a random permutation of the input lines to standard output.
text: Writes a random permutation. There is no --seed. Reproducible draws use --random-source with a file of bytes. -i ranges over integers and -n limits the count. shuf is GNU-only; it is not a sort.

title: sleep
summary: Pause for NUMBER seconds.  SUFFIX may be 's' for seconds (the default),
text: Pauses for a duration. GNU sleep accepts a decimal and the suffixes s, m, h, and d. An invalid interval exits non-zero. It is not a scheduler. timeout is the tool that stops another command.

title: sort
summary: Write sorted concatenation of all FILE(s) to standard output.
text: Orders lines. -s disables the last-resort full-line comparison. -S sets the initial memory buffer (default unit 1024 bytes; M is 1,048,576). -T sets the temporary directory. --parallel defaults to available CPUs capped at 8. Exit status 1 means a -c check failed; 2 means an error.

title: split
summary: Output pieces of FILE to PREFIXaa, PREFIXab, ...;
text: Splits by lines, bytes, or into N chunks. -d uses numeric suffixes. -n r/N round-robins lines, so a file with one line puts everything in the first piece. --filter runs a command per piece. BSD split does not have this -n syntax.

title: stat
summary: Display file or file system status.
text: Prints metadata with a format string. GNU uses -c. BSD uses -f for the format, which is the single most common portability break. stat -f here means filesystem status, and %T can say ext2/ext3 on ext4.

title: stdbuf
summary: Run COMMAND, with modified buffering operations for its standard streams.
text: Adjusts C FILE buffering by preloading libstdbuf.so. The binary contains the strings LD_PRELOAD and libstdbuf.so. cat and dd do not use FILE streams. tee resets its own buffering. -iL is rejected with status 125. It is ELF-only and GNU-only.

title: stty
summary: Print or change terminal characteristics.
text: Changes or prints terminal settings. This course does not run stty against the session terminal, because a bad mode breaks the terminal. Read the manual before using it in a script. It is not a file-permission tool.

title: sum
summary: Print or check BSD (16-bit) checksums.
text: Historic BSD (-r) and System V (-s) checksums. cksum -a bsd and cksum -a sysv cover the same algorithms. Do not use sum for a new integrity check. The output width and algorithm differ between -r and -s.

title: sync
summary: Synchronize cached writes to persistent storage
text: Asks the kernel to flush cached writes. With no operand it syncs all filesystems the process may sync. -f syncs the filesystems that contain the named files. It does not prove a drive's firmware finished the write.

title: tac
summary: Write each FILE to standard output, last line first.
text: Prints lines in reverse. It is GNU-only; BSD users often use tail -r. -s sets a separator, and the separator stays attached to the record, which makes the reversed bytes look surprising until you inspect them with od.

title: tail
summary: Print the last 10 lines of each FILE to standard output.
text: Prints a suffix, or follows a file with -f. -F follows by name and retries. -n +K starts at line K. GNU negative counts on head are a different feature. Follow mode runs until it is killed; bound it with timeout.

title: tee
summary: Copy standard input to each FILE, and also to standard output.
text: Copies stdin to stdout and to files. -a appends. The manual notes that tee adjusts its own buffering, so stdbuf does not control it. It is the coreutils way to save a copy of a pipeline without a shell process substitution.

title: test
summary: Exit with the status determined by EXPRESSION.
text: Evaluates an expression and exits 0 or 1. Bash's builtin test shadows /usr/bin/test. -s is true only for a non-empty file. The manual lists test among the commands whose 0 and 1 are answers. Use spaces around operators.

title: timeout
summary: Start COMMAND, and kill it if still running after DURATION.
text: Runs a command and sends it a signal when the duration elapses. The default exit status is 124 if the command was signaled. --preserve-status returns 128 plus the signal, 143 for SIGTERM. It is GNU-only. macOS users install gtimeout.

title: touch
summary: Update the access and modification times of each FILE to the current time.
text: Updates timestamps or creates an empty file. -d takes a date string and -r copies a timestamp from another file. -c does not create. BSD touch uses -t for a timestamp and does not accept GNU -d.

title: tr
summary: Translate, squeeze, and/or delete characters from standard input,
text: Translates or deletes bytes from stdin. It has no file operands. Character classes such as [:upper:] are locale-sensitive. A UTF-8 character is more than one byte, and tr will rewrite each byte that appears in the set. It is not sed.

title: true
summary: Exit with a status code indicating success.
text: Exits with status 0. The shell builtin is what an unadorned true usually runs. /usr/bin/true --version prints the coreutils banner. Useful as the command argument to nice or timeout when you need a known status.

title: truncate
summary: Shrink or extend the size of each FILE to the specified size
text: Sets a file to a size. Extending a file creates a hole when the filesystem allows it, which is why du and stat then disagree. Shrinking discards the tail from the directory entry's point of view. It is GNU; it is not dd.

title: tsort
summary: Write totally ordered list consistent with the partial ordering in FILE.
text: Topological order of a list of pairs. Input is one pair per line. A cycle makes it fail. It is the coreutils tool for a dependency order, not a general sort, and the input is not a Makefile.

title: tty
summary: Print the file name of the terminal connected to standard input.
text: Prints the terminal name connected to stdin, or fails when stdin is not a terminal. Pipelines and this capture environment are not terminals, so tty exits non-zero. The manual lists tty among special exit statuses.

title: uname
summary: Print certain system information.  With no OPTION, same as -s.
text: Prints kernel and machine facts. -srm is enough to identify the capture class without a hostname. -a includes the nodename. It does not print the coreutils version; ls --version does that.

title: unexpand
summary: Convert blanks in each FILE to tabs, writing to standard output.
text: Turns runs of spaces into tabs. -a converts all runs, not only leading ones. -t must match the tab stops expand used, or the round trip changes columns. It is byte-oriented.

title: uniq
summary: Filter adjacent matching lines from INPUT (or standard input),
text: Collapses adjacent matching lines. It does not search the whole file; sort first. -c counts, -d prints duplicates, -u prints uniques. -i folds case. GNU -z matches sort -z. sort -u is not the same once keys are involved.

title: unlink
summary: Call the unlink function to remove the specified FILE.
text: Removes one name with unlink(2). It does not remove directories. It does not take -r. If another hard link remains, the data remains. rm is the tool with prompts and recursion.

title: users
summary: Output who is currently logged in according to FILE.
text: Prints login names from utmp. This sandbox has no logged-in users, so the output is empty and the status is still 0. An empty line is not an error. who shows the same records with more columns.

title: vdir
summary: List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
text: vdir is ls -l under another name, from the same package. Use it only when you want that default. Scripts should call ls -l so the format is explicit on systems where vdir is absent.

title: wc
summary: Print newline, word, and byte counts for each FILE, and a total line if
text: Counts newlines, words, characters, bytes, and the longest line. -l counts newline bytes, so a file with no trailing newline can have a last line that -l does not count. --files0-from reads NUL-separated names. --total controls the total line.

title: who
summary: Print information about users who are currently logged in.
text: Prints utmp records. With no logins it prints nothing and exits 0. It is coreutils on this Ubuntu. uptime is not, even though people mention them together. Do not parse who to authorize a user.

title: whoami
summary: Print the user name associated with the current effective user ID.
text: Prints the effective user name. It still works when logname fails. It does not print the uid; id -u does. It is not a security boundary.

title: yes
summary: Repeatedly output a line with all specified STRING(s), or 'y'.
text: Repeats a string until the pipe closes. The usual close is SIGPIPE. With pipefail the pipeline can exit 141. Without pipefail the status is the reader's status. Bound it with head. It is not a load generator you should leave running.
